subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to continue my remarks on Bill C-14. As Hon. Members know, the Bill is an outcome of the Budget presented by the Minister

October 30, 1986
Excise Tax Act
of Finance (Mr. Wilson) earlier this year. It seeks to increase the sales and excise taxes on numerous items.
In my remarks last night I detailed at some length where the increases were applied. I also noted that since taking office the Government has dramatically increased sales and excise taxes. It increased as well the numbers of items on which sales and excise taxes are placed. Because of the Conservative Government, we now pay increased taxes on soft drinks, fruit juices, chocolate bars, vitamins, insulation material, gasoline products, construction materials, and other manufactured products.
I enumerated as well the regressive nature of the sales and excise taxes. They are essentially hidden taxes. When a consumer or taxpayer purchases an item, he or she does not see the percentage being paid in taxes-the nickels and dimes and very often dollar bills. As opposed to the provincial sales tax which is added on to an item when it is purchased, federal sales and excise taxes are hidden in the cost of the item purchased. Therefore we call it a back-door tax. It is a tax which takes money out of the back pockets of taxpayers. They are not aware that they are paying it. The average Canadian family pays hundreds of dollars every year in these taxes. In fact, since the Government was elected, the average Canadian taxpayer pays some $800 more per year in hidden taxes.
Of course the Government has justified Bill C-14 and other measures which increase the tax load of the average Canadian on the basis of fighting the deficit. In my remarks last night I stated that we in the New Democratic Party are also concerned about the deficit. The amount spent every year just to service our accumulated debt is money which cannot be used for other purposes. We disagree with the Government, as we did with the Liberal Party when it was in power, that Canadians are living beyond their means and that we are spending too much money on social programs. I take issue with those remarks. Compared with other industrialized countries, the percentage of our Gross Domestic Product spent on social programs is one of the lowest. It is lower than that of Italy, Ireland, Holland, Denmark, England, Germany, Sweden, Norway, and France. When I refer to "social programs", I mean pensions, family allowances, education, health, and income support programs. As a percentage of everything produced in Canada, we spend less on these programs than other OECD countries. It is not that we are living beyond our means, certainly not compared with other industrialized countries.
Why do we have the present deficit? In my remarks last night I suggested the reason for the deficit of today was that we have not had a fair taxation policy. We have not been taxing in a fair way large corporations and wealthy individuals who can afford to pay taxes. Those who are able to pay taxes have not been paying their fair share. Billions of dollars have been lost because we do not have a fair taxation policy in Canada.
One example I used was that of a teller with the Royal Bank of Canada. In 1983 that teller would have paid more in actual dollars and cents in taxes than did the Royal Bank of Canada,
although it made over $300 million. To rub salt into the wound, the Government of Canada gave the Royal Bank of Canada over $6 million in tax credits that same year. Not only did it have a profit of over $300 million and did not pay one cent of tax on it, it in fact received money from the Government. I just use it as one example. One could examine the taxes paid by all banks and find that they were certainly not carrying their fair share of the load.
Another example is the youth who pumped gasoline for Shell Oil in 1983. He paid more in dollars and cents in taxes on his meagre income than did Shell Oil in the same year. Had we had a fair taxation system, we would not have the deficit of today.
We can lay blame on the Liberal Government of previous years. Indeed it must accept a large amount of responsibility. However, the Government changed in 1984. Canadians were expecting a different direction, but all they have seen is a continuation of the same direction of philosophy, that is, the trickle down theory. That theory indicates that if corporations such as Shell Oil and the Royal Bank of Canada are doing well, eventually the profits will be recirculated in terms of new investment and new capital equipment, the creation of more jobs, and so on. However, we have seen that the trickle down theory in fact has not worked. The extra profits, tax breaks, and loopholes given to large corporations have not produced the types of jobs they were supposed to produce. Much of the extra profit went into corporate takeovers and mergers. The Canadian economy today is one of the most centralized and concentrated economies in the western world. In large part corporate takeovers are financed by the existing tax regime. In other words, they are financed, aided and abetted by Canadian taxpayers. We in the New Democratic Party not only point to the unfairness and inequities of the system but demand change or genuine tax reform.
The Minister of Finance rose in the House and presented a paper on tax reform. We certainly welcome this move toward tax reform. If there is a genuine desire on the part of the Government to institute a fair and equitable tax system, it will have our full and total support. Unfortunately, we suspect that the Government will be playing a shell game.
Indeed, the Minister will present a tax reform package that will do away with some loopholes, that will attempt to simplify the tax system and indeed that might even reduce the tax rates ordinary Canadians will pay. However, we strongly suspect that while the Minister of Finance will reduce tax rates for ordinary Canadians, he will increase, as he has in Bill C-14, the amount of taxes average Canadian families will pay out of their back pockets in hidden sales taxes.
This Government has relied more than previous Governments on hidden sales taxes as a source of revenue. In fact, the Government has suggested that it will soon introduce a form of a value added tax or a business transfer tax. We are awaiting the Government's proposals in this area. Previously the
October 30, 1986

Minister of Finance stated to us in the Finance Committee that he would have a paper ready as of April of last year. April has come and gone. Then the paper was to be ready in September. September has come and gone.
We suspect that there will be dramatic increases in sales taxes while there will be some small decrease in the amount of income tax Canadians will pay. It will be a shell game designed to confuse Canadians so they think they are paying less in taxes when in actual fact they are paying more. We in the New Democratic Party opposed Bill C-14 for the reasons I have enumerated and for other reasons that my colleagues will mention in the debate on this Bill.

Madam Speaker, Bill C-14 before the House today arises from the budgetary measures of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), and its purpose is to amend the Excise Act and various taxes in this country. To rephrase this for our listeners, it means tax increases for all Canadian taxpayers.
Madam Speaker, when introducing this Bill, the Hon. Member for Trois-Rivieres said that its purpose was to reduce the deficit. Later on I will explain and show how the Conservative Government should have proceeded to reduce the deficit, but first I would like to consider the general aspects of this Bill and how they relate to the May 1985 Budget speech and the February 1986 Budget.
Let us consider all those other taxes the Government has decided to impose and what the consequences will be for Canadians. First of all, I think we all remember that this Government has decided to modify the indexation of the basic deduction for dependents, and this applies to all taxpayers. After trying to subtract 3 per cent from the indexation of Old Age Security benefits and family allowances, it proceeded to do the same for the tax tables, thus affecting both the taxpayer and his family.
On February 26, the Government changed the rules for the married exemption in the year the marriage takes place. In the Budget Papers tabled by the Minister of Finance in February 26, we see that the Government has just saved $20 million. This means taxpayers are paying 320 million more to support the Conservative Government's wasteful spending.
In 1986, we also had a 3 per cent surtax that was expected to produce $550 million and will cost taxpayers $1.2 billion in
1987,	$1.26 billion in 1988, $1,325 billion in 1989 and $1.4 billion in 1990, and all because of the 3 per cent surtax.
Madam Speaker, if we consider the increase in federal sales tax in the February 26 Budget, taxpayers will be paying $700 million more in 1986, $1.05 billion in 1987, $1,125 billion in
1988,	$1.2 in 1989 and $1.3 billion in 1990.
Raising the tax on tobacco will give the Government about $150 million more annually between 1986 and 1990. Then we have the changes in the airport tax, another increase, and there
Excise Tax Act
again, the Government expects to collect about $15 million annually over the next five years.
Madam Speaker, we recall that in the 1985 Budget, this Government started to attack the people of Canada, our families and our senior citizens. First, it decided to tax candy and softdrinks. It went on to tax pet food and was adamant in its refusal to grant exemptions for guide dogs for the sight-impaired.
At the same time, the Government decided to take advantage of illness in this country and tax drugs in Canada. I am referring to over-the-counter drugs like aspirin and cold remedies. The Government decided to tax them all. When children get sick, the Government is delighted, because it gets more tax revenue.
The same applies to surgical and dental instruments and X-ray machines, so that when Canadians go to the dentist, they will be paying more as a result of the taxes levied by this Conservative Government.
Wood stoves, the entire building industry, solar heating systems, insulation panels and tubes ... Madam Speaker, about the only thing that has not been taxed by this Government is the air we breathe, and that is only because it has not yet found a way to do it.

My colleague for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme), who has a long experience of the House of Commons, tells me, and he is certainly right, that it will soon happen. Our own Brian will soon find a way to tax the air we breathe.
Madam Speaker, taken all together, the two fuel tax increases, two tobacco and alcohol tax increases, and two sales tax increases on soft drinks, food products and health products have had an enormous impact on the purchasing power of Canadian men and women.
The figures I am going to quote show the impact of the two Budgets of the Conservative Governement. A family with an income of $15,000 will see its taxes or purchasing power increase by 23 per cent. However, a family with an income of $200,000, who must have friends somewhere, will have a tax increase of 1 per cent.
Madam Speaker, is it any wonder that the Governement has lost so much ground in the polls? Why is it that the public has no confidence in the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney)? It is very simply because of this inequity, incompetence and social injustice.
If we look at single parent families with two children and an income of $15,000, we see that, as a result of the two Budgets, they will have to pay $248 more in taxes. For a family with an everage income of $200,000, the increase will be $418. As for

October 30, 1986
Excise Tax Act
taxpayers with an income of $150,000, their tax increases will be proportionally much lower in view of their ability to pay.
We have been told that the purpose of this Bill is to reduce the deficit. Everyone in this House, whatever his party, agrees that the deficit must be reduced. However, we disagree about how to do it.
Madam Speaker, it would be appropriate to remind the House about the scandalously wasteful spending of the party opposite. While this Government was asking Canadian families to accept lower than anticipated increases in their family allowance cheques, it was spending $55 million to change the colour of the Armed Forces uniforms. The difference between the Conservatives and the Liberals is a matter of priorities. All the Conservatives said: We prefer to have lower family allowances and spend $55 million to get a blue uniform for our soldiers; this will make them better. We, Liberals, say: It is better to maintain our family allowances; our soldiers are competent enough and they will not improve because of the colour of their uniforms. It is only the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who believes that appearances are all important, but the Liberals disagree.
There is also the matter of the additional $400 million spent by the Government to send more Canadian soldiers to Europe. This is again a matter of priorities. I am not against our participation in NATO, but I do disagree with the priorities of this Government since this happened at the same time that the Governement wanted to de-index old Age security pensions. That is the difference between a Liberal Government and a Conservative Government. A Liberal Government wants to protect Canadians. A Conservative Government wants to reward its wealthy friends. We can understand why. In all our history, the Conservatives have not been in power very long, and when they have formed a Government, they have taken whatever they can get. We have only to recall the former Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion. He was doing quite well for himself!
If we want another case of wasteful spending, Mr. Speaker, and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) is now in the House, the Governement took away $30 million from 50,000 Canadian workers, including 21,000 in Quebec, people who had paid unemployment insurance premiums for 20 or 30 years and who had accepted early retirement so that younger workers could get a part-time job, and in other areas, such as Trois-Rivieres, where companies closed down and laid off their employees, these workers were entitled to benefits from their pension plans, to which they had contributed, in addition to unemployment insurance benefits, but the Conservative Government took away their cheques every month without any warning and with the support of the Minister of Employment and Immigration. It has been estimated that these people are losing $10,000 a year because of the Conservative Government policy, yet at the same time the Reichman brothers used these funds to buy Gulf with Petro-Canada. This is where Quebecers in Montreal East were taken to the cleaners-$800 million worth of tax havens.
As you can see there is no limit for the rich, but as far as the Conservatives are concerned no such preferential treatment can be extended to most poor people and middle income families. Their motto is: The rich will get richer, the poor will get poorer. So much for the Conservative Government strategy.
I just referred to the case of the Montreal East Gulf refinery where we were taken for a ride, where Conservative Members had to give up in frustration after openly admitting they had been hoodwinked by their Prime Minister and others. So now we learn that the Government wants to spend $80 million to operate yet another refinery in the Maritimes. In this case they claim the American market is there to be tapped, but when Gaz Metropolitain was prepared to re-open a refinery with a minimum grant the then Minister of Employment and Immigration flatly refused. They said no at the time, but now they sing a different tune because the refinery is located in another province. Some $80 million right down the drain!
The collapse of banking institutions has to be the unparalleled precedent: roughly $1 billion was handed out to 200-odd depositors, including ten or so with investments of at least $2 million. They got their money back straight from cut-backs in family allowances paid to mothers. Their allowances were slashed just so the Government could come up with $ 1 billion cash for depositors who had at least $60,000 in these banks, not for taxpayers with a mere $10, $100, $500 or $1,000 to their names. At least $60,000 is the amount all Canadians had to pay to make up for the mistakes and blunders of this Conservative Government, they have had to make do with smaller family allowances, pay taxes on drugs and a sales tax on materials. That is where money could have been saved in order to reduce the deficit, rather than coming up with a bill that strikes at the whole Canadian people.
It was recently reported-and the scandal is getting bigger and bigger that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) himself helped waste another $41 million simply by transferring, to his own constituency, a penitenciary that was to be built in the constituency of Drummondville, and the cost is to be $41 million. At the same time, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) will not refund the $30 million to Canadian taxpayers who paid unemployment insurance premiums. That is a scandal. Will you call that sound management? Instead of introducing with Bill C-14, they should have prevented that squandering of money.
We could talk about the cost of receptions given by the Prime Minister, about his travelling expenses, about the cost of caviar. If the Prime Minister likes to eat caviar, let him pay for it. But making taxpayers pay for his caviar receptions in Europe, that tops it all. He could share the eating habits of Canadians in other areas. At his own expense, he may well treat himself whenever he wishes, but on the backs of the Canadian people he should exercise more restraint.
Remember the wasting of money when the Prime Minister was master of ceremonies for the President of the United States. He stated then: Let the party, let this reception cost

whatever it may. But that was the taxpayers' money. And now, in order to pay for all those errors, those blunders, as we recall that famous consultation he had with business people, labour unions, at an astronomical cost, and then the Government turned around and did the opposite of what those people had recommended. Well now, they have to introduce legislation to increase the taxes to be paid by all Canadians, thereby strinking at everybody. We know very well that some people do smoke. Those people are taxed to the hilt, having to pay a bundle in order to cover the $41-million cost of transferring the Prime Minister's penitentiary. People who drink alcohol, liquor also pay a heavy cost for this Tory Government's squandering of money.
Our unemployed who lost those $30 million also pay a high price for the foolish actions and the boobs of a Government anxious to salvage failed banks, something that could have been foreseen with a better administration and better managers.
There is something else that should also have been discussed instead of having this Bill to reduce the deficit, rather than hitting the whole population with indirect taxes-Madam Speaker, I have two minutes left-the changes to the RRSPs. We know that in 1983, RRSPs cost $4.9 billion to Canadian taxpayers, and who in the population can save the nicest amount of money for their retirement? Will it be a family earning between $15,000 and $20,000 with 2 or 3 dependent children? This is a regressive measure.
Madam Speaker, in view of my limited time, I would like to show Hon. Members what will be the consequences of the new changes to RRSPs, as proposed by the Government, changes that raise the ceiling. The way the Government went about it-and this reminds me, since the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) is here, of the amendments to prevent workers from benefitting fully from their unemployment insurance-it was indeed the scheme in which the money was paid by middle-income people, by workers. But if you withdraw the money from your tax-exempt RRSP, because you earned a lot of money, you can withdraw the full amount, and you are still entitled to unemployment insurance benefits. That is Tory justice. But to come back to this new measure, and I would like to conclude with a few words on RRSPs, when someone with an $8,000 taxable income contributes $1,000 to an RRSP, thereby decreasing his tax liability, this costs the taxpayers $346. But when someone earning $80,000 contributes the $5,500 maximum, it will cost the taxpayer $3,323.
Madam Speaker, I conclude on that, and this shows clearly that this Prime Minister, this Tory Government are there to favour the rich. They have no understanding whatever of the less privileged people, they have no appreciation, no compassion whatsoever, for middle-income people.

Madam Speaker, I would like to ask a question of the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart). I agree with most of his criticisms of the tax proposals of the Government. However, I would like to remind the Hon. Member that for 42 of the 49 years between 1935 and 1984 we had Liberal Governments. It was Liberal Governments which really developed, expanded and refined our tax system to its present state. The Conservatives are making it worse.
The Member has criticized the Conservative Government because the tax changes which it made benefit the rich at the expense of the poor. The Liberals were in power for three and a half of the years between 1980 and 1985. The following corporations paid not one cent in corporation taxes in at least one of those years: the Royal Bank; the Bank of Montreal; the Argus Corporation; the Power Corporation headed by that great friend of the Liberal Party, Mr. Desmarais; Investors Group, also headed by Mr. Desmarais; and the Roman Corporation, that giant corporation headed by that great Conservative who came here as a poor immigrant and is now a multimillionaire. How does the Hon. Member explain the failure of the Liberal Government to ensure that those and many other corporations paid their fair share of taxes?

I am pleased that the Hon. Member is clearly asking what should have been done today. Why should a reform be undertaken today? In the first place, social programs-We started just as in the case of tax shelters or taxation, to bring in improvements year after year to social programs, to the

Madam Speaker, I had anticipated that some Conservative Members would want to defend the tax increase proposed in the Bill under consideration, Bill C-14. I am deeply disappointed that not one of those Members, not even the Secretary of State of Canada and Minister for Multiculturalism (Mr. Crombie) is willing to assume the task of defending a tax hike.
I wish to remind all Hon. Members that the sales tax is going to be raised once again by 1 per cent. This means that the new rates will be 8 per cent for building materials and cable television services, 15 per cent for alcoholic drinks and tobacco and 12 per cent for other taxable goods.
Madam Speaker, last week, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) promised in his speech that he would make some changes in the fiscal reform so as to make it more progressive and fairer for ordinary Canadian families. Unfortunately, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) did not comment on any of the actions of his Government since the September 84 election. As a matter of fact, during those first two years of the Conservative Government, instead of introducing a fairer tax system, they have implemented a tax system which is less fair, very much so, than the previous one. And clearly, Madam Speaker, there were quite a few problems already with the existing system when they came in power.
Madam Speaker, we have mentioned the fact that the various changes brought about by the Conservatives have resulted in a tax increase of $1,300 a year for the average Canadian families in September 1984. And where has this tax burden been mostly applied? The tax burden was weighted heavily towards excise and sales tax, instead of using personal and corporate income tax. This new emphasis means that most of the new taxes are regressive.
Madam Speaker, I can give you the exact figures, the figures we arrived at during the tax inquiry we started early this year.
The November 1984 economic statement increased sales tax and excise taxes for the average Canadian family to the tune of $350 per year. In the May 1985 Budget, the Government again imposed a 1 per cent increase in sales tax, which cost the ordinary Canadian family an average of $325 per year. Finally, in the February 1986 Budget, another $170 per year, so that we now have a total of $845 per year. And all this in only two years' time, Madam Speaker! During that same period, income tax increases which, as everybody knows, are more progressive and more equitable for families whose
Excise Tax Act
financial circumstances may vary, these increases totalled only $385 per year, so that 69 per cent of our tax increases were covered by excise and sales tax and only 31 per cent by income tax.

I raise that because I believe these heavy tax increases are a preview of what the Government intends to do in the future. Last week the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) stood in the House, as his colleagues are not prepared to do now with Bill C-14, to tell us that great days are ahead. He rose to make a promise that I am sure we will hear often between now and the 1988 or 1989 election. The Conservatives will say: "We will cut taxes, is that not wonderful?" Let me tell ordinary Canadian taxpayers, including those in the Niagara Peninsula, that they should hang on to their wallets. They may find a few dollar bills in their front pockets, but they had better watch what the Conservatives are taking from them as a result of the increases in sales taxes that the Government is contemplating.
The Government is anticipating a new form of sales tax called the business transfer tax. Western Europe and other countries which have used this kind of tax have found it very costly in terms of what it takes out of the pockets of consumers. The advantage to the Government is that it can bring in a new tax while cutting the tax rate and appearing to reduce taxes. However, the tax base is spread at the same time, until far more is being taken from that particular source of taxes than before.
Our tax probe inquiry last spring took me and my colleagues from the New Democratic Party to every corner of the country. We went as far as Yellowknife, Yukon, Newfoundland, Vancouver and Victoria. We went to every part of the country to talk to people about their concerns about the tax system. We talked to small business people, consumers, trade unionists, business people, tax experts and people in municipal and provincial Governments. They told us what should be no secret, that is, there are real problems with our tax system. The present sales tax is a bad system and should be abolished. We should be looking for alternatives. I accept that one alternative is some form of value added tax such as is being proposed by the Minister of Finance. However, that said, let us be very specific and not use it as a Trojan horse, that is, take an enormous amount of new revenues from families on ordinary incomes who are having a heck of a time surviving in today's economic environment. Yet that appears to me to be what the Government has in mind.
The Government is saying it is going to plug loopholes and cut personal income tax rates. People in low income brackets do not have a lot of loopholes. On the other hand, they are not going to get many cuts because the cuts the Government has in mind, in terms of marginal tax rates, are the rates of 43 per cent, 48 per cent and 54 per cent which, in gross terms, between federal and provincial Governments, are charged on upper income tax earners. There is not much benefit for people

October 30, 1986
Excise Tax Act
with ordinary incomes. They may receive a few dollars but nothing much more than that.
In terms of corporate tax, the Minister has made some ineffectual suggestions, dare 1 say, about perhaps increasing the tax on corporations. We know the Government has now begun to realize that Canada, like the United States, has to plug corporate tax expenditures and if it does so, it can reduce the rate of tax on corporations. That in itself is not necessarily objectionable. What is objectionable is the Government's suggestion, and it was quite explicit in the budget paper of May, 1985, that it wants a corporate tax reform which will be revenue neutral.

To be revenue neutral means that instead of increasing its revenue through corporate taxes, the Federal Government will take no additional revenue from the corporate sector. Certain loopholes will be eliminated. Corporate tax expenditures will be eliminated or else limited or reduced, but generally, businesses will be compensated by such a reduction of their tax rates that they will not pay any more taxes than they do now.

We have seen, and we have cited these figures in the House on many occasions, just how little increased revenue the Government anticipates from the corporate tax side over the course of the next few years until 1990 or 1991. As I recall, it is something in the order of about $2 billion. We are faced with the heavy expenditures of the Government of Canada, with the difficult situation with regard to the deficit and we have a situation where tax expenditures, many directed to the corporate sector, are currently worth about $28 billion a year. If these tax expenditures were eliminated today, it would virtually wipe out the deficit. Therefore, it seems irresponsible to me for the Government to say, as it said in May, 1985, from which it has not backed away, that it is going to get rid of tax expenditures to corporations, but instead of using the money to limit the tax burden on other Canadians or using it to cut the deficit, it is going to turn around and give back the money to the corporations.
What the Government is saying, and it is quite clear, is that the Minister of Finance and his colleagues now look on the business transfer tax, on a reform of the sales tax, as a great big cash cow which it can milk in order to get new revenues to plug the deficit or to do other things it feels are important, such as putting prisons in the Prime Minister's riding.
It is clear that although this tax is to be called a business transfer tax, there is no mistaking who will pay. The consumers will pay in the first place because more than half of final demand obviously comes from consumers buying goods and services. Second, it will be paid for by consumers because, to the extent the tax is paid by businesses buying goods or services from each other, they will pass on those costs to the consumer in the end, and in the end it is the consumer who will pay.
Let us take the example of a bushel of wheat which is grown in western Canada. It sells at a domestic price of $5.50 or $6. It is then shipped to central Canada and milled into flour. Perhaps as flour it is worth $12. Then it is taken to a bakery and turned into bread and in the form of bread it may be worth $30 or $35. It is then shipped to the foodstore where it is finally sold to the consumer and that $6 worth of grain winds up as $50 worth of bread which is purchased by the consumer. On the value added at each stage, no matter how the calculation is made-and I accept the business transfer tax is slightly easier than the proposals for value added tax on the European model-there will be a tax at a certain rate on the farmers' sale, on the value added by the farmer in taking a bit of grain, fertilizers and so on, and turning it into wheat. So there is value added on the miller, on the baker, on the wholesaler and, quite possibly, at the retail level, although I am not sure whether that is contained in the proposals of the Minister of Finance because we have not seen them as specifically as we might. Therefore, the rate of tax at the end is going to be equivalent to a hidden sales tax on either the wholesale or the retail value of the entire commodity, and any transactions between businesses will still result in an increase in tax which will ultimately be paid for by the consumer.
The question then is, what will the rate be? Will there be any kind of diminution for people who are on lower and modest incomes? We have to look at Bill C-14 and what the Government has done in order to see just what its current stance is on this very important issue. In the first place, as I said a few moments ago in French, since 1984 the Government has increased taxes on the average family by $1,300, and 70 per cent of that increase has come from increases in sales and excise taxes. That is an increase of $845 a year. Has the Government done anything in order to lighten the burden of those increases on people in modest circumstances so as to make it a more progressive system? The answer is, virtually not at all.
I want to draw to everyone's attention that a sales tax by its definition is proportional to what people spend. If we have large exemptions, such as the current exemption on food and other necessities of life, then in fact it does tend to deal more with the disposable income of people after they have met the necessities of life and, therefore, it is to that extent somewhat more progressive. A future business transfer tax, if the base is going to be broadened, I presume is likely to touch such things as rent, food, fuel oil or other basic necessities of life. We are going to have to wait and see. It is difficult to judge the Government's proposals until we get that far.
But let us take that $845 increased tax burden in sales and excise tax on the average family and ask what the Government has done in order to try to moderate that. What it has done is to bring in a sales tax credit. That sales tax credit is, if I recall correctly, worth $150 a year to a family, and the value to a single person or single mom is worth $100 a year. That is not a heck of a lot of relief when we look at the average bill of $845. In fact, what we find when we look at the figures is that the
October 30, 1986

impact of the sales tax increases has been relieved by up to about $1,500 a year for people with very modest incomes. Beyond that point we see that this is not a proportional tax. It is a regressive tax. A regressive tax is a tax which hits more heavily those in modest circumstances than it does those in better circumstances.
The following are figures which have been drawn from the report of the National Council on Welfare. It must be noted that we are looking only at the impact of the increases in sales tax and not at the over-all impact of sales tax, which I believe we should be doing. According to the National Council on Welfare, the cost of the tax increases in 1985 and 1986 on a couple with two children at the $15,000 level will be an increase of $215. However, after the sales tax credit is taken into consideration the net cost as a percentage of family earnings will be 0.4 per cent. In other words, the sales tax credit is relatively effective in ensuring that those people at that income level, which is below the poverty line, are not heavily hit by this new tax. However, the sales tax credit expires just above that income level. When we consider a family with an income of $20,000, we see that the tax increases are estimated to be $269. I think that is a bit low. There is no relief from the sales tax credit at all for such a family. Therefore, the net cost is the same as the gross cost, which amounts to 1.3 per cent of the family's earnings. As we move into higher income brackets, for instance the $30,000 bracket, the sales tax increase is equal to 1.2 per cent of family earnings. At $40,000 it is equivalent to 1.1 per cent of family earnings; and at $100,000 it is equivalent to 0.9 per cent of family earnings.
I wish to say, Madam Speaker, that with your knowledge- [Translation]
With your knowledge of Quebec society, for instance, you will see that it is much easier for someone with a family income of $100,000 a year to pay .9 per cent more of his income in sales taxes than it would be for someone with a yearly income of $20,000, just above the poverty line, with a wife and two children, to pay 1.3 per cent more of his income in sales taxes.

That is the problem we face. By its actions the Government has brought in a sales tax credit which is so paltry that it does not do anything to stop the regressivity of the current sales tax increases which were levied in 1984 and 1985, except for those people with incomes below the poverty line.
If the Minister had said last week that a major change in the sales tax credit, or an equivalent measure, was needed to ensure that on all incomes up to, let us say $40,000 or $45,000, the net impact was progressive as opposed to regressive, then I, as a New Democrat on behalf of my Party, would have said that we will seriously look at the measure. However, that was not done. Instead, the Minister has come forward with some

bold words about tax reform on the one hand. On the other hand, as a result of his actions in Bill C-14, he is taking us in a direction which is the exact contrary. Bill C-14 is nothing but a hangover from the last Budget.
In terms of this value added tax, the business transfer tax which we will have, the Canadian federal sales tax currently taxes only 30 per cent of the potential base in terms of private consumption. In Denmark, for example, the value added tax is imposed on 80 per cent of private consumption. In France and West Germany the figure is 29 per cent, and in the U.K. it is 60 per cent-

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is with a great deal of interest that I look at the items which fall under the Excise Tax Act being presented in Bill C-14.
Over the last two years the Government has imposed the largest tax increases ever upon Canadians. The Government promised fair and equitable measures. It promised to be open and to listen to the people and reflect their concerns. Unfortunately, the Government has been a great disappointment to many Canadians.
When Members are out in their ridings, and as we talk to our constituents, many of us sense their great unhappiness, their cynicism and their lack of trust in legislators. Money is tight and jobs are scarce. Students do not know how to make decisions with respect to their futures because the whole situation is so unstable. The concerns of the people being expressed in the ridings as we meet them, whether we are Conservative, Liberal or New Democratic, indicate a great sense of instability.
What accounts for this instability? We need to look no further than the Government of Canada. Many people watch the proceedings of the House, especially during that silly period between two o'clock and three o'clock. They think that is all we do here. The ridiculous comportment of many people in the House has left the Government in general, and the public in particular, very disturbed. It is the job of the Opposition to test and check, to ensure that we are responding in our proper role. All the ordinary people see is the external behaviour. They do not appreciate that we also work at this hour in the House to study the Bills the Government presents. If members of the public were to think about what the Government is proposing to do in Bill C-14 they might become even more cynical. The Government has literally emptied the pockets of the low and middle income people of Canada. The disposable income available to make the wheels go round, the

October 30, 1986
Excise Tax Act
money people need to spend on goods is no longer there. We are seeing a slow-down in the economy. What I am saying sounds simplistic. I want it to be simple because I want those who look at the bottom line of budget sheets to stop and realize that these figures represent actual dollars in the pockets of everyone. The tax dollars which are being pulled out of these pockets, most of it in hidden taxes, is disconcerting to these people.
It is simplistic of the Government to say that it has modified the indexation of the tax table by 3 per cent. This will not look like much in the ordinary person's pocket as they go to fill out the required forms. When we look at what that does in terms of the nation we see that it is taking $570 million out of the collective pockets of taxpayers. We must also consider the 5 per cent and 10 per cent surtaxes which were imposed in the November and May Budgets respectively. They represent another $550 million which will be taken out of the pockets of taxpayers.
The Government eliminated the 1973 federal tax reduction which cost the taxpayers another $490 million. The Government levied a 1 per cent increase in the sales tax rate in November of 1984 which removed $1 billion from the pockets of taxpayers. That is $1 billion in taxes on goods on which people were not used to paying taxes previously. It was increased again in May, 1985 to the tune of $990 million. In fact, we do not even seem to care where we put our zeros at this point. The poor taxpayer is hounded and he does not know where to stop or start.
The Government put a sales tax which was broadened across the spectrum to include pharmaceutical products and consumer products. This included construction goods, cable and pay-TV services, alcoholic beverages and tobacco. On construction, taxable goods were increased from 7 to 8 per cent; cable and pay-TV from 7 to 8 per cent; alcoholic beverages and tobacco from 14 to 15 per cent. On other taxable goods, the increase was from 11 to 12 per cent. The sum total is billions of dollars.
When I talk about those kinds of taxes and we look at the 1986 Budget with an additional 3 per cent surtax, the additional 1 per cent sales tax, the alcohol and tobacco excise tax, it amounts to close to $5 billion of taxes taken out of the economy, which is the highest in our entire history.
Yet we were able to find a billion dollars of relief for the banks. We were able to find practically $1 billion in tax concessions to Gulf. We were able in many ways to cut back the middle and lower income people and to give bonuses to the well to do. I agree that incentives for productivity in our society are very important. But there is a need for fairness and equity. Canadians want, deserve, and expect fair play from their Government. This is not what they have received. The right to increase RRSP limits from the original $5,500 to $7,500, which is going up to $15,500, will cost a $40 million loss to the Treasury this year. It is very nice for people in the upper income tax bracket who can take out savings and protect
themselves for their older years in life. It is very important that we allow for that, but we have to allow for it on an equitable basis. We have to start looking at how we cover everyone with proper pensions that are portable and vested and have a cost-of-living adjustment. This applies to not only those who presently have pensions, but also to those who are not covered.
The capital gains exemption now covers art, boats, and apartments in Florida or Paris. There is a capital gains protection of up to $500,000, which is half a million dollars. That is five times $100,000. There are people who do not even know how to write these kinds of figures, and they are the largest percentage of the population. In this Chamber we were elected to represent all strata of society, not just upper income earners. This Budget is a Budget for upper income earners. It is true that the argument is that you must protect those upper income earners because they are the people who make the wheel go round. Do they really? Who is the mass of society going out and purchasing the goods and the services? It is not the small 3, 4, or 5 per cent at the top of the scale. It is the majority of Canadians.
I would like to suggest that this is a totally unacceptable Budget, with five billion dollars more in taxes with still no control of our deficit. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has announced that he will be $2.5 billion short of the target, so there is something wrong with the planning that we see in front of us. The Government talks with a great sense of pride about what it has done in the communications and the cultural field. The Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) Government has feebly attempted to place this high priority, but it has forgotten a few of the things it has done. In the Government's first Throne Speech there was absolutely no mention of Canadian culture. In the 1984 Economic Statement and in the subsequent May Budget of 1985, we witnessed cut-backs to the cultural industries of a grand total of $122 million. The Government felt guilty over its previous cuts, and in February of this year it allotted $75 million to fund a number of cultural initiatives. I am pleased that it did that. It was just including and increasing some of the work that we had already started. Even with that addition there was a shortfall of $47 million. In July the cultural community again shuddered as there were rumours of more cuts. This was to correct an error in the Minister of Finance's budget calculations. There were cuts of $10 million to the CBC; $210,000 to the National Art Centre; $1.6 million to the National Film Board; and $1.95 million to the Canada Council. That adds up to an additional $13.7 million. All the hopes of February had been dashed. This week we heard that the CBC in its upcoming Budget for 1987-88 may be cut an additional $50 million. In this light, the Government stands there and says that it is committed to the cultural industries, it is going to protect our cultural sovereignty, and it is going to see that Canadians can stand proud and tall and count themselves in the cultural stream. I would suggest that actions speak louder than words. This Government has been very famous for shaking your hand happily beforehand and then finding ways to apologize in a backhanded way.
October 30, 1986

I alluded to the sales taxes, excise taxes, alcohol and tobacco taxes, and manufacturing taxes. Many people in Canada travel by air. Effective May 1, 1986, there will be a tax on domestic air travel, which will be limited to a maximum of $50, while the tax rate will increase from 9 to 10 per cent. The tax will be extended to tickets sold outside of Canada on or after August 1, 1986. That is very good for our tourist industry. But at least we avoided the major part of Expo. Expo was a great success for which we can all be grateful.
On the telecommunications side, there has been added a telecommunication programming service tax called the TPST tax. This tax applies to television equipment provided to customers of cable and pay-television services. It also applies to equipment used by hotels and other closed-circuit broadcasts. The TPST was increased by 1 per cent to 7 per cent in the 1985 Budget. The proposed legislation will increase this tax by another 1 per cent to 8 per cent effective April 1, 1986. The Government is certainly finding many ways to enable the Minister of Finance to reduce the deficit effectively. The only problem is that he has not controlled it yet, even with all these excessive taxes.
The 1985 Budget may be perceived as having changed the method by which federal sales tax is levied on motive fuels. There is a sales tax which continues to be imposed as an ad valorem tax, that is, 12 per cent after April 1, 1986. But it is calculated as a specific amount per litre. The specific amount is adjusted quarterly, according to the industry's selling price index as published by Statistics Canada.
The Ways and Means motion to Bill C-14 is intended to clarify how the sales tax calculation is to be made. We can see some very significant increases in here through the federal excise tax on non-commercial motive fuels which will be at 1.5 cents per litre. The 1985 Budget increased the excise tax on gasoline and aviation gasoline by 2 cents per litre effective September 3, 1985. This tax is scheduled to increase to 4.5 per cent on January 1, 1987. We are looking for ways to discourage tourism. When you look at the cost of gasoline, tourists must receive an incredible shock when they find out how much it costs to fill their tanks. I wonder if these costs do not offset some of the difference in our dollar calculation. They are a disincentive. I would suggest that the tourist industry has to work twice as hard to attract tourists because of our hidden taxes. They return home and wonder what happened to their money.
I am not pleased with the way in which the Government has chosen to direct this piece of legislation. I speak on behalf of the people in my riding of Mount Royal. They are concerned about jobs, the future, and the ability to live on a decent scale. In order for them to do that, they require justice and equity in the tax system.
I encourage government Members to examine their budgets and the way they are levying taxes, in the interest of everyone, not just the well to do.

Madam Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question. It provides me with an opportunity to say a few things which I think need to be said.
Very few of us realize the very difficult management task of the CBC. If one stops to think about the CBC, one realizes that it is quite an extraordinary national expression of Canadians. It expresses our diversity, as well as the beauty and grandeur of our country. It certainly has some problems. Nothing in Canada is perfect; nothing in Canada is totally beautiful. However, we should stop to think about the activities of the CBC. It broadcasts in French and in English across the land, from Newfoundland to B.C., from Cap d'Espoir to Vancouver Island; from the U.S. border to our friendly borders in the far North. Its services cover the Inuit and other native peoples, as well as our diversities in major regions, both in radio and in television. We should also think about the fact that on the international scene the CBC is an instrument of Canadian national policy of which we should be extremely proud.
There has been a $75 million cut to the CBC plus $10 million in new equipment which was required, for a total of $85 million in the November statement. There was an additional $10 million cut when the Minister of Finance made a mistake and announced $500 million. He was short and went to find places to cut, so he cut the CBC again. He has now cut another $50 million, or it is an anticipated increase. Therefore we are talking about $145 million in cuts.
Let us also look at a serious matter which is of concern to everyone in the House. I am referring to the $57 million which we cannot find and has not been accounted for. The Auditor General is concerned about it, as is the President of the CBC, Mr. Juneau. Mr. Dye and Mr. Juneau are trying to locate that money. The problem in terms of its loss was the institution of a new budgeting procedure.
My answer to the Hon. Member would be a return question to him. What right had the Government in 1985 to allow the CBC to go into a very complex budgeting procedure, a new fangled highly complex system, without ensuring that a back-

up system was in place or that the Department of Communications was doing its proper job in supervising the CBC?
We must be very cautious when we talk about the CBC and in a sense protective, but at the same time we must demand the kinds of answers we as legislators require.

Madam Speaker, I listened to the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) and thought she made an excellent speech. She outlined the very regressive nature of the taxes which are being heaped, with each succeeding Budget, upon low and middle income Canadian families. However, I would be interested in her view of the speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) a week or so ago. He talked about tax reform and trying to reduce income tax scales. The first two Budgets of the Government seemed to be geared toward reducing taxes for large multinational oil companies, increasing taxes for low income families, deindexing the income tax scale for families, deindexing personal exemptions, deindexing the family allowance, and so on. Does the Hon. Member see the Government making a 180-degree turn on its taxation policy? Madam Speaker, it is my intention to speak very briefly and only on one aspect of Bill C-14, that being the excise tax imposed on airline tickets.
The point I wish to make is that the Government of the day is responsive to the representations of the citizens of Canada.
Some time ago, the excise tax on airline tickets was 7 per cent, I believe, or perhaps 8 per cent, and there was a cap on it, a maximum tax payable of $35. About a year ago, or perhaps a little more, changes were made to that excise tax in order to generate more revenue. Of course, the Government had a very good point when it argued that additional revenue from aviation was required because the amount of money that was being collected was nowhere near enough to provide the necessary services to aviation.
At that time, the excise tax was raised to 9 per cent, but the cap of $35 maximum was removed. This resulted in taxes on an airline ticket from the town in which I reside, Yellowknife, to Frobisher Bay on the other side of the Territories of about $150. This, of course, was ridiculously high. The airfares in that area are high to begin with and to put a $150 tax on top of that is ridiculous. The situation was the same for all long distance transportation in Canada. In those areas where ticket prices on a per mile basis are higher, the northern and remote areas of the country in particular, the removal of the tax cap was particularly onerous.
As a result of the removal of this cap, many representations were made to the Minister of Transport of the day, the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), by chambers of commerce, municipalities and even the Province of British Columbia. I was worried for a while because I thought that the Government might not do anything about this. However, it did turn out well. The Minister of Transport was responsive to the wishes of the citizens and so was the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson).
The legislation that is before us, Bill C-14, increases the excise tax to 10 per cent but reimposes the cap. This is what the people wanted. They did not mind paying their fair share in taxes on airline tickets, but they did not want to pay $100 or $150 in taxes on expensive tickets. They wanted the cap reinstated, and that is what Bill C-14 has done. Therefore, I would like to take this opportunity to thank both the former Minister of Transport and the Minister of Finance for acceding to the wishes of Canadians and in particular those who live in the far reaches of the country.

benefits will go to wheelers and dealers, people who drive BMWs and Porches and who live in Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver. Very few people who live in the vast expanses of Canada such as those which lie within his particular constituency will benefit.

Madam Speaker, first I think the Hon. Member is wrong to assume that the increase in excise taxes will only pay for the exemption on capital gains. That, of course, is wrong. Excise taxes come in and go out of general revenue. One could equally argue that a tax of this nature will pay for old age pensions or will go into the unemployment insurance fund. The Consolidated Revenue Fund receives money from many sources and there is a number of ways the money goes out of the fund.

I do not know the exact proportion of people who can benefit from it, people who cannot benefit from it or people who can benefit from it in the future in any one riding. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we have before us a Bill whose life was somewhat interrupted. Bill C-14 implements changes to sales and excise taxes

October 30, 1986
announced in the Budget Speech of February 27, 1986. I think a brief resume of the nature of these changes will be instructive to understanding the effect they will have on the Canadian economy and the Canadian taxpayer, particularly those at a lower level of income, on whom this tax will bear regressively.
The 1 per cent sales tax increase applies to a number of essential goods and services, for example, construction materials, where the rate goes from 7 per cent to 8 per cent. On other taxable goods it goes up from 11 per cent to 12 per cent. While neither I nor my Party need shed too many tears over the increase in taxes on alcoholic beverages and tobacco, both of them destroyers of human life and longevity and both, after all, the popularly styled sin taxes, which frankly are set at a level which might easily be increased with over-all benefit not only to the exchequer but also to the health of the nation, yet they are taxes people pay. When we look at the over-all impact of the excise tax and federal sales tax increase, we cannot believe it will be anything but negative. The increase in these indirect, hidden taxes, as they are sometimes known, is part of the Government's strategy of increasing taxes. Indeed, it makes a very powerful contribution to the implementation of that strategy.
My Party has calculated that the tax burden on the average family since the Progressive Conservatives came to power has increased in the order of $1,300. That is based on an annual income of $35,000 for a family with two dependent children. It is useful to contrast the level of increase in taxes on the average family with the level of increase in taxes on the average corporation. Here the disparity is quite dramatic. I frankly believe that when the history of the 1980s is written, unless there is some dramatic move by the Government, something rather more than what was promised in the recently tabled proposals for tax reform, this decade will go down as the period in which the average family in Canada was called upon, and called upon disproportionately, to shoulder the burden of deficit fighting. That will be seen as a sad commentary on the orientation of the Progressive Conservative Government.
The increases which have taken place already, together with that proposed by this measure, constitute $845 of the $1,300 figure I referred to. The November 1984 Economic Statement adds approximately $350 a year. The May 1985 Budget adds $325 a year. The February 1986 Budget adds $170 per year for the average family. Because of the ratcheting effect of successive increases, this is beginning to take me back to my point about taxes being paid on taxes. So we have a situation where the average family in Canada is being called upon to bear the burden of this Government's deficit fighting initiatives.
At this point I wonder if I might call it one o'clock, Madam Speaker.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR BAN ON CIGARETTE ADVERTISING

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Of course he will know that Mr. Fonyo is now dying of lung cancer. Will the Minister respond positively to Mr. Fonyo's appeal? Knowing that tobacco companies are spending $200 million a year to undo any good that the Minister's pro-health campaigns are doing, will he respond positively by putting an end to the disinformation campaigns, with a total ban on cigarette advertising?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: REQUEST FOR BAN ON CIGARETTE ADVERTISING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think all of us received the news of Mr. Fonyo Senior's illness with deep regret. Regarding the ban on advertising, as I told the Hon. Member earlier, that issue has many more implications. It is not simply a matter of banning advertising so that people will no longer smoke, thereby ending lung cancer. Obviously that which the Hon. Member continually puts forward is not the complete answer.
October 30, 1986

Mr. Speaker, will the Minister not respond favourably to the latest campaign of Physicians for a Smoke-Free Canada? As the Minister knows, Members of Parliament will receive black-edged cards when their constituents die from tobacco-related diseases. Will the Minister respond favourably to the plea Physicians for a Smoke-Free Canada made this morning when they stated that they are tired of government inactivity, and specifically requested a ban on advertising as a first step toward controlling smoking in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, regarding the argument that there has not been government activity in the last two years, I really do not think I have to defend that once again in the House of Commons. The Hon. Member knows as do most Hon. Members that, from my perspective, if it were possible, the route I would like to take would be to ban cigarette advertising. I constantly hear the argument that Finland has done so. I spoke to the Minister for Social Security of Finland two days ago. The Finns had to amend their Constitution in order to ban cigarette advertising so that it would not be an abrogation of press rights. I would suggest to the Hon. Member that, when she wants to put facts before us, she should put the entire package before us so that we can look at it in that sense.

Mr. Speaker, two weeks ago Premier Peckford promised Newfoundlanders that he would "blow their minds" with an announcement. The announcement was made. It did not blow their minds, it boggled them. Hear, hear!

could Petro-Canada not do what this company says it will do with the refinery?

subtopic: FREE TRADE WITH UNITED STATES-POSSIBLE EXCLUSION OF AGRICULTURE
FREE TRADE WITH UNITED STATES-POSSIBLE EXCLUSION OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of State for External Affairs.
Yesterday, the Union des producteurs agricoles du Quebec met with the three political parties in Ottawa to object to the inclusion of the farming industry in the free trade discussions with the United States.
My question is this: Can the Minister now assure us that agriculture will not be included in the free trade negotiations between Canada and the United States?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pat Carney (Minister for International Trade):
subtopic: FREE TRADE WITH UNITED STATES-POSSIBLE EXCLUSION OF AGRICULTURE

speechtext:
Remember the leadership in Saskatchewan, Lome.

October 30, 1986

Mr. Speaker, the answer is yes. The UPA has said that the dairy industry and sectors such as poultry and pork production would be destroyed by a free trade agreement between Canada and the United States.
Can the Minister tell us once and for all whether or not the farming industry will be on the negotiation table, because the UPA would like an answer now.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pat Carney (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there are a number of elements involved in the negotiations. I would like to point out to the Hon. Member that a poll released today showed that 57 per cent of Canadians support the free trade initiative of this Government.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Finance. Last night before the Finance Committee, the Chairman of the Continental Bank stated that in order to preserve the jobs of his employees he had no option but to seek a merger with a foreign controlled bank since, without legislative changes, large Canadian non-bank financial institutions such as Sun Life and National Trust could not acquire the Continental Bank. Will the Minister bring in changes to the ownership provisions for Canadian financial institutions in order to enable control to remain in Canada should a similar situation develop in the future, or is he satisfied that the loss of Canadian control is the only way to save jobs in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is asking about a future policy about which he is curious. I can guarantee him that in the next month or two we will bring forward our policy which will endeavour to maintain Canadian control as best we can, create jobs, and increase the further competitiveness of our banking system.

subtopic: EXISTENCE OF NEW MARKETS FOR PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
EXISTENCE OF NEW MARKETS FOR PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister or the Acting Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
Last year around this time, Gaz Metropolitan and the Quebec Government were asking the Conservative Government for assistance, in keeping the Gulf refinery open in Montreal East. The Energy Minister at the time answered that there was no market.
Could the Minister inform the House today how he was able to find an export market when a year ago, there were no markets to keep the Gulf refinery in Montreal East operating?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerald S. Merrithew (Acting Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
subtopic: EXISTENCE OF NEW MARKETS FOR PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it should be noted that in the ongoing negotiations for the Come-by-Chance refinery, no federal moneys are directly required. All of the output of this particular refinery will go to the United States thanks to very good negotiations by the Province of Newfoundland.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister doesn't have his facts straight. The Government is going to sell at a discount price of less than $2. And besides, Gaz Metropolitan was merely asking for permission to purchase the Gulf refinery.
Could the Minister explain what has changed in the energy sector to make him say today there is a market in the U.S., while a year ago, the Energy Minister at the time told us there were no markets?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerald S. Merrithew (Acting Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it should be well known that the purchasing company will purchase the entire output of that particular plant. We think it has found its own market niche and we welcome that kind of opportunity for economic activity in Come-by-Chance.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of the Environment. The Haida people and Canadians from coast to coast want to know if the federal Government is prepared to offer fair compensation to the
October 30, 1986

loggers and logging companies on Lyell Island and in South Moresby so that the area will be protected. Can he tell this House, the Haida people, and the people of Canada, whether or not he is prepared to make that offer today?
Good question.

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is a good question. I provided the answer in this House some weeks ago when I said to the House and, through it, to Western Forests Products Ltd. that the Government of Canada would be very predisposed toward sitting down with them to negotiate the value of the timber licences and to reasonably compensate the company for them.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Minister for that answer. However, as he knows, logging is going on on Lyell Island today in areas under negotiation for designation as Canada's highest priority national park. Is the Government going to take the necessary steps to get the cooperation of the B.C. Government to stop that logging before it becomes the South Moresby National Slash Park?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the situation is delicate. I do not think one needs to resort to exaggerated rhetoric to underscore the problem. The Government of Canada is deeply concerned about what is happening in the South Moresby area. I do not think it would be an overstatement to say that violence, even death, is possible if this thing gets out of control. We are working behind the scenes, quietly, reasonably and co-operatively, with the Government of B.C. and the Haida themselves to see whether we can avert disaster.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF GOVERNMENT DECISION ON MINIMUM TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance, or in his absence, for the Minister of State (Finance).
The Conservative Governement has imposed a minimum personal income tax, but not a minimum corporate income tax when we know that thousands of profitable corporations pay no taxes in Canada.
Must we conclude, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Finance was not aware of certain figures which are essential to prepare any budget or implement any major tax initiative? Or must we conclude, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Finance and his Government deliberately and unduly favour these companies, some of which are very large?
Oral Questions

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF GOVERNMENT DECISION ON MINIMUM TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the issue of a minimum tax for corporations is of course being examined in the ongoing consultations on tax reform. I will tell the Hon. Member that 13,000 Canadian corporations paid tax last year that had never paid tax before.
I will also tell him that the American system of a minimum corporate tax is not working very well and produces trivial amounts. We have to look at this carefully because there is no easy answer.

subsubtopic: POSSIBL E GASOLINE PRICE INCREASE-DELAYED IMPLEMENTATION ON BEHALF OF CONSUMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
Last Spring, when the price of crude oil went down by 60 per cent, the Government was very slow to react. Canadians had to wait three months before noticing any change in the prices at the pump.
According to a Canadian Press release from Calgary, there will be an increase in prices within a month.
Can the Minister assure us that the Canadian consumers will have the same three months of grace before there is any increase at the pump?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: POSSIBL E GASOLINE PRICE INCREASE-DELAYED IMPLEMENTATION ON BEHALF OF CONSUMERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member knows, there is no constitutional authority for the federal Government to set prices. We can only try to ensure that the market-place is truly competitive. In that regard, the Director of Investigation and Research in the Competition Branch is monitoring petroleum markets directly. If the Hon. Member has any evidence of efforts to manipulate the market to the disadvantage of consumers, she should let us know and we will take action immediately.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO GIVE EQUALITY OF TREATMENT TO CANADIAN CONSUMERS
GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO GIVE EQUALITY OF TREATMENT TO CANADIAN CONSUMERS
speechtext:

October 30, 1986

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of the Environment. In order to avoid the possibility of violence and death, which the Minister referred to a moment ago, will he stand in his place today and publicly ask the Government of British Columbia to stop the logging on Lyell Island until such time as successful negotiations can be concluded?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):

Member calls upon me to make now. I can assure him that we are pursuing the matter with vigour. The position of the Government of Canada is clear and it has been conveyed clearly to the Government of B.C.

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF TORPEDOES FROM UNITED STATES

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. Since last Saturday the Kerkhoff-Hyundai consortium has been raising polluted debris from the bottom of the Fraser River near the Pattullo Bridge and dumping it just over the edge of the pilings into the flowing river, thereby seriously endangering the fish habitat.
Why is the Department of Fisheries permitting this dumping when no environmental impact studies have been done and no public hearings have been held?

October 30, 1986
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have not yet received a report from officials on the West Coast about the problem raised by the Hon. Member. If there is any evidence of contraventions of Sections 31 and 33 of the Fisheries Act, appropriate action will be taken immediately.

subtopic: MARKETING OF FRESHWATER FISH-SENATE COMMITTEE REPORT
MARKETING OF FRESHWATER FISH-SENATE COMMITTEE REPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
