subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext: When the House rose at one o'clock, the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Parry) had the floor.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to reclaim the floor, even in the somewhat disruptive aftermath of Question Period, because it gives me the opportunity to emphasize again to the House the way in which the Progressive Conservative Government is garnering its increased taxes principally upon the backs of ordinary Canadians and at the expense of the budgets of ordinary Canadian families.
Before we rose for lunch I was at the point of coming to the division of increased taxes under the Government. The figures are instructive and I hope the Government will observe and absorb them because they are surely a signpost showing the principles the Government is following in its tax gathering campaign.

October 30, 1986
Excise Tax Act
There has been an increase of $6.7 billion in sales and excise taxes since the Government took power, compared to $3.3 billion in personal income tax increases, and a meagre $1.4 billion in increases in the corporate income tax. The only conclusion one can reach when considering these increases together is that they are regressive.
We know that the sales and excise taxes that go into the purchase cost of most goods that are purchased in Canada- apart from food and refreshments obviously-are taxes that are paid in a much more equal fashion by the poor and the wealthy than any other form of tax. Not only have repeated studies analysed this tax as being regressive, I have not even heard anyone on the government side contradict this analysis. Unlike the personal income taxes which are progressive in the sense of being paid at a higher rate as one's income increases, sales and excise taxes are regressive.
For example, if a person with an annual income of $15,000 buys the same mix of taxable goods and services as someone who earns $75,000 a year, they pay the same amount by these indirect taxes. It should also be pointed out how these taxes are concealed from the taxpayers, namely the consumers. Unlike the provincial retail sales taxes which are added as a percentage of the price and are visible to the consumers, except in the case of beverages in some provinces, federal sales taxes are hidden from the consumer because they are included in the final price of the item. For example, families with an income of $20,000, who are not eligible for the so-called refundable sales tax credit which the Government has introduced, are the ones who will be hit hardest by this combination of sales and excise tax increases.
It is worth-while calling the Government's bluff on this question of the refundable sales tax credit. Our Party is not against such a tax credit and believes it does something to offset the increased taxes, but let me point out the analysis of the National Council of Welfare which has calculated that while this form of tax relief reduces the over-all burden considerably, it does not fully offset the cost of that increase. The $50 and $25 for each child will offset most of the increase, perhaps, for families who are in the $10,000 to $15,000 income range, but those with incomes below even $20,000 will be paying more in tax even after the refundable sales tax credit has been factored in.
It is no secret to those who study economics that this diverts money from consumer spending. Indeed, the Conference Board of Canada has calculated that the increases will assist in slowing down personal expenditures by Canadians-that is, no expenditures-from a growth rate of 5.2 per cent in 1985 to 2.7 per cent in 1987. The National Council of Welfare has pointed out that over the last five years, with the exception of the wealthy and, gratifyingly, the very poor, on the average Canadians have experienced a decline in their purchasing power. I believe this is a trenchant criticism of this increased tax measure. When this is allied with the fact that over the last eight years Canadians have experienced a drop in their real
wage income, their real available spending power is also declining.
This must also be juxtaposed with statements by the Progressive Conservative Government concerning the need for economic growth. The restrictive effect that these increased taxes have on consumer spending will, of course, have an adverse effect on economic growth over-all.
I want to relate what we have seen the Government table in Bill C-14 to its suggested plans for tax reform and point out some of the inconsistencies. It is not my purpose to deny the possibility that the Government may indeed have had a change of heart or, perhaps as some of its back-benchers might say, suffered a change of heart. The fact is that there is a clear divergence between the actions of the Government in tabling Bill C-14 and its stated intentions, at least in the statement by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) on October 23, 1986. The statement that the Government needs more consultation time was instructive. Perhaps the Government wanted more time to elapse so it could garner tax at higher rates before introducing any measure which might lead to some loss of tax revenue in one of the three major tax accounts.
The Minister of Finance stated that he intended to reduce the rate of personal income tax in relation to over-all revenue. He felt that this could be done by seeking higher revenues from the corporate and sales tax systems. We can applaud an increase in the corporate taxes as a means of ending some of the outrageous selective tax preferences which my Party is now daily highlighting in the House, and with very good response from Canadians, I might say. Those measures have enabled many corprorations to avoid completely the payment of tax at the same time as their income statements and balance sheets are showing their increasing health. At the same time the stock market is showing in the clearest way possible that these corporations, which are in fact flourishing and prospering, are failing to make a contribution to the tax system.
Looking again at the sales tax system, it is difficult for my Party to see where further increases can be imposed without further increasing beyond the degree to which we are presently condemning the regressivity of that system. I think there is some fear of the imposition of a business transfer tax, a modified version of the value added tax, now endemic in other jurisdictions and, indeed, generally adopted within the European Economic Community, because that is in the statement as well. Similar products should bear the same rate of tax and the sales tax burden should be spread more equally across goods and services. We have here what has been referred to as "smoke and mirrors" and what has been referred to as "front-pocket donations and back-pocket extractions". As we have seen in the past, and as a well known satirical piece points out, the net result is that lower and middle income tax payers in Canada are going to pay. It is they who will make up the difference.
October 30, 1986

The over-all unfairness of the system is bolstered by the increase in sales and excise taxes, the hidden taxes, more regressive taxes which are difficult to administer, inflationary and, frankly, it is difficult to see how any business transfer tax could be introduced without essentially spreading some of the negative characteristics we have pointed out in the federal sales and excise taxes with, of course, the exception of the positive aspects the "sin taxes" have of discouraging the use of those products which are obviously harmful to all of us.
With respect to the business transfer tax, a value added tax by any other name, we have not seen anything concrete proposed, so perhaps it would be appropriate to leave that tax, even though it might cause an increase in the number of companies collecting by fifteenfold, and return briefly and finally to the federal sales and excise taxes. By 1988, revenues from the federal excise taxes and duties will have risen over 1984 by almost 90 per cent. That, I think, in a word, sums up the degree to which the Government is shifting to a form of tax which has been condemned by commentators right across the ideological spectrum in terms of economics, as a tax which is really counter-productive to the economy and one which is less than fair to those people who bear the largest share of the tax burden, and those people we must be concerned with, the ordinary Canadian family.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased with this opportunity to speak on Bill C-14, an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act. The purpose of this Bill is to increase certain taxes, which means that Canadians will again have to pay more for certain consumer goods, including manufactured goods and petroleum products.
To find out what might be of interest to Canadians in a Bill, you read what the Minister or his Parliamentary Secretary had to say about it. 1 will therefore refer to yesterday's Hansard at page 878, where the Parliamentary Secretary, speaking on behalf of the Government, introduced this budgetary measure.

I found it interesting that the Parliamentary Secretary for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Vincent) spoke for exactly 10 lines on the Bill itself. He said the Bill arose out of the Budget of February, 1986 and from the Ways and Means motion tabled on June 11 of this year. The essential and substantive part of his speech reads:
Excise Tax Act
The purpose of this Bill is to increase federal sales tax in certain areas. An increase of 1 per cent will raise sales tax on construction materials from 7 to 8 per cent, on alcohol and tobacco from 14 to 15 per cent and on other commodities from 11 to 12 per cent.
That is all we heard about Bill C-14 because for the rest of his speech he, true to form for a real good Tory, made political and partisan comments. I read it twice and underlined it trying to find further comments on Bill C-14, and there was nothing.
To be fair to the Parliamentary Secretary, perhaps he did not want to, or was not capable of doing what he should have done, and that is explaining what Bill C-14 was all about, the principle of it. But his speech was all style and little substance. So I will try, with all humility, to cover what the Bill intends to do. I will try to go along with my usual parliamentary habit and clarify somewhat what is in this Bill.
First, the Bill is a federally manufactured sales tax increase. This tax of 1 per cent will add tremendously to the costs of manufactured goods. I want to give to the House an appreciation of the impact of this tax. In his speech, I must admit, on page 879 in Hansard, the Parliamentary Secretary said:
-this Conservative Government and their Prime Minister are acting in a responsible manner, that we know where the money we spend is going.
That is fine, but he says further on that the Government announced in its last Budget that:
A family of four earning less than S15,000 will get $ 150 tax credit.
He enlarged on the great generosity of the Government and how lucky Canadians were to be allowed to receive $150 tax credit if they earn less than $15,000. I looked at my notes, which were quite substantial, to see what the facts are. What are the cumulative effects of the main tax measures introduced by the Tories since they took power in 1984? To find out one must go back to the November 1984 Economic Statement, and the respective Budgets of May 1985, and February 1986. If one goes through that exercise one will find that increases in taxes have been substantial.
However, for the couple with two children earning $15,000, the family to which my hon. friend referred yesterday, we find that because of the modified indexation of 3 per cent, because of the additional 5 per cent and 10 per cent surtaxes, because of the elimination of the 1973 federal tax reduction, because of the modification of child benefits, the family allowance, the tax credits, the exemptions-all those matters put together- that family will have to pay $190 more in tax than it paid in 1984. This shows that, indeed, the $150 is not sufficient even to cover these costs.
If we look further we will see that there is a 1 per cent increase in sales tax rates effective November, 1984; a 1 per cent increase in sales tax rates effective May, 1985; and an increase in the so-called sin taxes on tobacco and alcohol levied in the same Budget. The sales tax base was also broadened by that Budget. There were increases in the RRSP limits, and there was the famous capital gains exemption from which, we know, a family with an income of $15,000 does not profit very

October 30, 198(
Excise Tax Act
much. When we add all of this together we find that the result comes to an additional $175 for these items minus, and I must be fair, $10, which is a possible deduction on capital gains that a family earning $15,000 may have. That is a hypothesis which I put out.
With respect to the February, 1986 Budget, there are additional measures. We see that there is a 3 per cent surtax which adds $10 to the tax bill of this same family. It takes care of the $10 they gained on the capital gains exemption. Then there is the refundable sales tax credit which was mentioned by the Parliamentary Secretary. There are increases in the tobacco and alcohol excise taxes which will cost this family another $40. When we add up all these figures, this family will pay $255 more than they paid in 1984, even taking into account the $150 sales tax credit. That is not what I call fair, equitable or responsible, which are the words used by the Parliamentary Secretary. I think they are unfortunate words. So much for the federal manufacturers' sales tax increase and its impact.
The next item with which I wish to deal is the alcohol and tobacco excise taxes. I think people who use alcohol and tobacco should be paying additional taxes because they add to our national health bills. They eventually cost us more money. We should try to capture this money from them so that we can look after their health if they do not wish to look after it themselves.
The next item I would like to refer to is the air transportation tax. Effective May 1, 1986, the tax on domestic air travel will be limited to a maximum of $50 while the tax rate will increase from 9 per cent to 10 per cent. The tax will be extended to tickets sold outside Canada on or after August 1, 1986.
The fourth item with which I wish to deal is the telecommunication programming services tax. This tax applies to television equipment provided to customers of cable and pay-TV services, and to equipment used by hotels and other closed circuit broadcasts. The TPST was increased by 1 per cent to 7 per cent in the 1985 Budget. The proposed legislation will increase the tax by another 1 per cent to 8 per cent effective April 1, 1986.
Then we come to the fifth item in the Bill which deals with the motive fuel tax. Members will recall that in the 1985 Budget the method by which federal sales tax was levied on motive fuels was changed. As a result, the sales tax continues to be imposed as a percentage or ad valorem tax. It is calculated as a specific amount per litre. The specific amount is to be adjusted quarterly according to the industry selling price index as published by Statistics Canada. Clauses 6, 7 and 8 of the Ways and Means motion to Bill C-14 are intended to clarify how this sales tax calculation is to be made. We all know that additional sales taxes were added in 1985 to the order of .32 cents per litre for regular gasoline; to .35 cents per litre for unleaded gasoline; to .36 cents per litre for premium gasoline; and to .29 cents for diesel. We also know that the sales tax increase as per the Budget of April 1, 1986, will be increased
by .329 cents for regular gasoline; .36 cents for unleaded gasoline; .37 cents for premium gasoline; and .302 cents for diesel.
The next item with which the Bill deals is with respect to tourist literature. The 1985 Budget exempted government-sponsored tourist literature from federal sales tax. Effective February 27, 1986, the legislation proposed here would extend the exemption to tourist literature acquired by boards of trade, chambers of commerce, municipal and automobile associations, and similar organizations. The exemption applies only to material that is of general as opposed to specific commercial nature and that is distributed to the public at large free of charge. I think this is a plus in the Bill.
The next item with which I wish to deal is the refunding of sales and excise taxes on motive fuels to diplomats. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) will decide who will receive such refunds. This Bill proposes to refund sales and excise taxes on motor gasoline and diesel fuels to eligible diplomats from countries that provide similar relief to Canadian representatives.
The eighth item in the Bill deals with tax collection by Revenue Canada. As an aside, I am going through the Bill in this way because I think that yesterday most of us missed the principle at hand here. I am trying to be as brief and as specific as I can. Therefore I hope Hon. Members will excuse me if I do not go into too many examples with respect to each one of these items. According to existing legislation, Revenue Canada officials can demand payment of taxes owing for an unlimited amount of time. The Ways and Means motion to Bill C-14 proposes to allow Revenue Canada to collect only that amount of tax that will be paid or will become payable within 90 days after Revenue Canada serves the taxpayer notice of its intention to collect.
The ninth item deals with a motive fuel tax rebate to farmers. This is a measure in which a great many Members are interested, and justifiably so. It is a measure which has been mentioned by many Members in their speeches yesterday and today. The 1986 Budget extended a three-cent-per-litre fuel tax rebate to primary producers for another year, or until January 1, 1988. Then, on April 30, 1986, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) announced that effective May 1, 1986, the tax rebate would be increased by another 2.5 cents per litre, for a total rebate of 5.5 cents per litre. The Government, and justifiably so, estimates that this measure will save farmers an aggregate $165 million over the next two years.
This is a laudable move, and something which is justified. I only wish that the trappers had been included in the same measure. There are quite a few people who make a living from trapping in Canada, and they should be allowed the same rebate and receive the same consideration from the Government. As was mentioned before in debate, unfortunately this has not come about yet. Being an optimist, I am hoping that
October 30, 1986

some day the Government will see fit to allow people who make a living from trapping to be eligible for this rebate.
The only difficulty is that the $165 million over the next two years is based on an estimate. It assumes that the rebate program will be fully subscribed. However, previous experience will show that this is a questionable assumption. Not all people are aware of the rebate and, therefore, not all farmers claim it. The Government, therefore, gets away with not having to pay it all. Nevertheless, it is there and people should know about it. It is a good measure and we applaud it.
The last and final item is the impact of this sales and excise tax Bill on federal Government revenue. According to the Government's figures, this increases and extends the fuel tax rebate to farmers over the next two years. It will cost $65 million in lost revenue for 1986, and $100 million for 1987. This is in addition to the $120 million of lost revenue indicated in the years 1986 to 1990 under the commodity tax measures. Those items will be shown in the eventual cost to the Government, and, therefore, will have to be authorized by the House.
I wish to end my few remarks by saying that we deplore the fact that Canadian consumers are again being asked to pay increased sales taxes and will have to bear the brunt of these measures. I plead with the Government that it not use these regressive tax measures to try to expunge the national deficit. The $150 sales tax credit is a good measure. It is not sufficient to allow those in the low income groups to really be protected from these additional measures. This reduces their take-home pay and their capacity to keep up with both inflation and the demands of their families. If the Government wanted to be fair, equitable and just, it should have come in with a sales tax credit of a great deal more than $150 for those families. That would have given them a little more relief and would not have used what I would define as very regressive measures in terms of their revenues.
I end my remarks on that note. I hope that the Government will be responsive to expanding that sales tax credit, which I think is a good measure, and will allow for those with low and moderate incomes to protect themselves against inflation and increasing taxes.

I congratulate my colleague, the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) for his usual eloquence and objectivity in his remarks.
Does the Hon. Member think it is fair-and I know he will have considerable comment about this-that a married couple with two children, whose income is $15,000, will have to pay an increase in taxes of $255 as a result of the economic statement of November, 1984, and the Budgets of 1985, and 1986. Does he think it is fair that the Tories want to go through with this regressive tax measure which will inflict that sort of pain on ordinary and low income Canadians?

Madam Speaker, I thought I made this quite clear in my comments, but I want to thank the Hon. Member
Excise Tax Act
for giving me a chance to repeat what I thought I said in my speech, namely that it is unfair, regressive and lacking in any equity whatsoever to force these families where four people have to live on a very low income of $15,000, an income that is below the poverty line-we recognize that today-and in absolute terms, below the poverty line means that they are constantly having a hard time making ends meet and even putting food on the table. God knows that the definition of poverty... We should make a distinction here between absolute and relative poverty. Without wishing to seem frivolous, absolute poverty-intellectually speaking-may be what the Conservatives are suffering from, but as far as ... Yes, you Tories are absolutely incapable of any kind of original thinking. But absolute poverty, aside from the Tory connotation, may mean being unable to support one's family. Relative poverty means one is poor compared with other people in the same environment. Someone can be poor, meaning that he is unable to keep up appearances.
I realize that the Hon. Member-
Beauharnois-Salaberry!

speechtext: -for Beauharnois-Salaberry (Mr. Hudon) has a good definition of poverty, but I was not referring to intellectual poverty. I was referring to poverty-
Not Conservative poverty!

-as an economic concept, and not as a lack of intellectual capacity or initiative. He is an expert as far as that goes. Initiative just may be something which helps people make progress. A Conservative does not have initiative and stays put, he does not move at all. Therefore it is not very hard to define.
I would like to tell my colleague from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) that I am very sorry indeed to see this regressive measure under which the Government will tax two-child families, couples with income as low as $15,000. I said in my remarks that the Government was supposed to use this sales tax credit measure to boost the income of those people and give them the money they need to make ends meet. That is all.

A supplementary question, Madam Speaker. I thank my colleague for giving such a clear answer to my first question. Since he gave a very good explanation in answer to the first question I put to him, I should like to ask him whether he can understand why the Progressive Conservative Party on the other side continues to introduce such regressive measures-against a couple with two children, earning $15,000 a year, therefore already below the poverty level as my colleague from Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) so eloquently put it a moment ago-whether he can understand why the Conservatives would want to promote this kind of tax measure.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the explanation is fairly simple. All we need do is look at the tables and figures to appreciate that poor and middle income families are hit

October 30, i 986
Excise Tax Act
hardest by sales taxes and regressive taxes. Couples with two children and an annual income of $30,000-let us refer to figures which are not quite as dramatic as the $15,000 mentioned earlier-did suffer as well because of the 1984-85 and February 1986 Budgets. Again I might enlighten the House with a series of figures I have here. A couple with two children and an income of $30,000 has to pay $245 more than in 1984 as a result of the 1984-85 Budget which reduced indexation by 3 per cent, added 5 and 10 per cent surtaxes, did away with the 1973 tax reduction, and changed family allowances, the tax credit. In addition, they have to pay $280 more because, as you will recall, the sales tax went up by 1 per cent in 1984 and by another 1 per cent in 1985 and the tax base was enlarged, which means another $280, and when we add to that the impact of the 1986 Budget and the 3 per cent surtax, the 1 per cent increase in the sales tax and what we call the sin tax on alcohol and tobacco. We end up with $630 more a year for a couple with two children and a $30,000 income.
If we look further-and this is the funny thing-if we look at a family with an income of $50,000, we see that, because of the capital gains tax exemption, these people are paying only $575 more. With an income of $50,000, they are therefore paying less than a family with an income of $30,000.1 wanted to point this out because when I mentioned this fact recently in a speech, a reporter told me that I had made a mistake. I replied that I had not because, according to the figures, a family with two children and a $50,000 income pays less in taxes today than a family with a $30,000 income.
Incredible!

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
It is indeed incredible. I repeat that a family with a $30,000 income pays $630 more while a family with an income of $50,000 pays $575 more.
When I look at the Tories, Madam Speaker, I tell myself that they are right to look embarrassed. Is it not embarrassing to be taxing the middle classes more than the rich?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments. Debate. The Hon. Member for Kamloops- Shuswap (Mr. Riis).

Madam Speaker, I realize that we are anxious to get this Bill into committee for thorough examination, but this is an opportunity for Members of Parliament to discuss Bill C-14 in principle. The Bill we are debating today imposes a whole set of new taxes upon Canadian citizens. When they purchase soft drinks at the end of the day, they will pay more federal taxes. When they pick up chocolate bars or packages of gum, they will pay more federal taxes. When they fill up their gas tanks on the way home, they will pay more federal taxes. If they purchase some food for their pet cats of budgie birds, they will pay more federal taxes. I could go on and on, but we are
actually discussing a new regime of taxes being levied by the federal Government upon Canadians.
Not only are these taxes vast, comprehensive, and all encompassing, they are sneaky. They are hidden taxes. People do not understand and recognize them unless they have listened intently to the proceedings in the House of Commons, read Hansard or read carefully some of the financial pages in our national publications. Average Canadian citizens are unaware of the sneaky attempt to levy additional taxes.
This comes at a very peculiar time. I listened with interest to the comments of the Minister when he introduced Bill C-14. He went on at some length about the need for the Government to obtain more revenue. Of course he was concerned about the deficit, as we all are. We are all deeply troubled by the size of the deficit facing Canada. He went on to explain that this was why the Government had to go to Canadian citizens-rich or poor, middle or low income earners, easterners or westerners, men or women- and ask them to pay more taxes. I make that point for the following reason. It is the most regressive form of taxation anywhere in the taxation regime.
Living in a northern climate, most Canadians will be purchasing winter tires or heavy duty winter batteries; most Canadians will be winterizing their automobiles and so on. They will be required to purchase these materials and therefore pay sales taxes. Everyone pays the same amount of sales tax on a set of snow tires which costs $150, for example. Whether they are very wealthy or poor, whether they are low or middle income earners, it is irrelevant. Therefore it is perfectly clear who is penalized most by these taxes-low and middle income Canadians. The same amount of money is levied upon everyone.
When corporate presidents earning $200,000 to $300,000 per year purchase snow tires, they will pay a few extra dollars as a result of Bill C-14. They will not notice it. It will not have a significant impact upon their lifestyles; as a matter of fact, it will probably have no impact whatsoever. However, when low income earners who are heads of households with two children and annual incomes of $15,000 purchase the same snow tires for their automobiles or trucks, they also have to pay a few extra dollars as a result of Bill C-14. It will have a significant impact upon those families. This is why we in the New Democratic Party will oppose Bill C-14 at every stage. If there is a need to raise money or revenue, there are more appropriate ways of doing it.
Why do I say "if there is a need"? It is because in introducing this piece of legislation the Minister made a point about the deficit. It is not surprising that we have an increasing deficit. When we look at the tax system, we find that there are tens of thousands of profitable Canadian corporations which pay no income tax to the federal Government year after year. As a matter of fact, in 1983 there were 79,196 profitable Canadian companies which did not pay a single penny in federal income tax at the corporate level. By the way, their profits combined were some $13.3 billion. In 1983, $13.3 billion went untaxed.
October 30, 1986

I suppose one of the reasons for the present deficit-and unfortunately it appears to be an increasing one despite the comments of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson)-is that our tax system is so incredibly inept, biased, and unfair that it allows $13.3 billion to go untaxed. This is not my figure. This is not our figure. Figures such as this one were brought to our attention as a result of our 1986 tax probe. Various organizations across the country provided us with information. In fact, the federal Government provided the information indicating that 79,196 profitable corporations paid no income tax to the federal Government in 1983.
We should also consider the fact that 64 of the companies which paid no federal income tax in 1983 had profits in excess of $25 million. These are not corner stores or small Canadian companies; their profits in 1983 were in excess of $25 million. It is not surprising the Government has trouble in terms of collecting revenue.
May I make a rather humble suggestion. Rather than penalizing Canadian citizens by increasing sales and excise taxes or by imposing what is being called a business transfer tax, which will be even more oppressive, the federal Government ought to give serious consideration to an immediate overhaul of the tax system at both the corporate and personal levels and ought to determine to what extent it needs to continue to raise more revenues on the backs of Canadian taxpayers.
I do not have to remind Hon. Members of the SRTC boondoggle. It was an attempt by the Liberal administration to encourage Canadian companies to participate in research and development. Because of its ill-conceived nature, this cost Canadian taxpayers somewhere in the neighborhood of $2 billion to $3 billion. I do not have to remind you, Madam Speaker, of the billion dollar bank bail-out or of the billions of dollars that have now been given to the multinational oil companies as a result of the removal of the PGRT. It has been estimated that as a result of that decision, billions of dollars will not be going to the federal Treasury over the next few years.
I suppose the most stinging indictment of all is the continued support of the Minister of Finance for the $500,000 capital gains exemption. There are very few countries in the world where one would find people whose incomes are derived from selling race horses, artifacts or Caribbean boats or from investing in the Hong Kong stock exchange going totally untaxed to the tune of half a million dollars. I am not aware of any country in the world which has carte blanche application of a capital gains exemption. I have never heard of such a country, but perhaps other Hon. Members are aware of other countries that have this provision.
I would like to tell the House about the general track record of the Government since it has taken office. If there is a hallmark of this Government, it would certainly be the fact that any increases in revenue tend to come by way of hidden
Excise Tax Act
taxes. Rather than making up-front increases to the personal or corporate tax levels, the Government imposes hidden taxes so that Canadians are unaware of what is going on. Now the Government is committed to introduce what would be a simply inappropriate type of tax, a value-added tax, or as the Minister of Finance has called it, a business transfer tax. It should not be called a business transfer tax because it is essentially a widening of the federal sales tax base.
At the moment, the sales tax base is restricted primarily to the manufacturing sector but the business transfer tax the federal Government will be introducing in the next few months will tax virtually every business transaction that takes place. Experts in the tax field have called this a massive tax grab. I do not know of one single tax expert who has not called it a massive tax grab, a licence to print money or another descriptive phrase of that nature.
The Government might be lowering the personal tax rate so that a few extra dollars get into the pockets of Canadians. While a few extra dollars might go into their front pockets, the Government will be reaching behind to pull a few hundred dollars out of the hip pockets of Canadians. This will be done through a hidden, sneaky tax called the business transfer tax. It is a very regressive step and one that will concern you, Madam Speaker, a great deal, unless it is introduced in the context of over-all, massive, comprehensive, total tax reform along the lines of that which occurred in the United States.
In the United States, there has been a shift away from the personal taxpayer to the corporate taxpayer. President Reagan himself has decided that $120 billion will be moved onto the shoulders of the corporate sector and off the shoulders of the personal sector. That is the kind of step that makes a great deal of sense.
The Government has been taxing and taxing Canadians. In the economic statement of November, 1984, the federal Government announced a 1 per cent sales tax increase that had previously been introduced by the Liberals. The Government also announced an increase in the petroleum compensation charge. In the May 1985 Budget, a 1 per cent federal sales tax increase was announced for January 1, 1986, and an excise tax on gasoline was to be increased by 2 cents per litre on September 3, 1985, and by 1 per cent per litre on January 1, 1986. A new excise tax of 2 cents per litre on diesel and aviation fuel was imposed. There was a broadening of the federal sales tax base to include candy, confectionary, soft drinks, pet foods, certain health foods, energy conservation equipment and pharmaceutical devices. An excise tax on tobacco was increased by 52 per cent in the May 1985 Budget and an excise tax on alcohol was increased by 2 per cent. In the February 1986 Budget, there was a 1 per cent federal sales tax increase for April 1, 1986. An excise tax on tobacco increased by 6 per cent. An excise tax on alcohol increased by 4 per cent.
Adding together all of these personal tax increases including sales tax, excise tax, gasoline tax and personal tax increases, it amounts on average to $1,350 per Canadian family. By a Canadian family, I mean a family of four with an average

October 30, 1986
Excise Tax Act
annual income of $35,000. As a result of two years of Progressive Conservative Government, each Canadian family is paying an extra $1,350 out of its pockets. That means that in every small community, whether it be Richmond, Kamloops, Chicoutimi, Carp or Hawkesbury, the average Canadian family is losing to the federal Government $1,350 each year, year after year.
What does this mean to the small businesses in those communities? It simply means that that money is not circulating in those areas. That money is down here being used for highly questionable expenditures like bail-outs to bank depositors.
I will never feel comfortable with the fact that the Government provided thousands of millions cf taxpayers' dollars to depositors like the Bank of America, Wells Fargo, the Bank of Japan, the Bank of Hong Kong, the Bank of Abu Dhabi and the Bank of Saudi Arabia. Did those banks really need to be bailed out by small Canadian taxpayers? No, Madam Speaker. As a matter of fact, this has not happened anywhere else in the world. Taxpayers' money has never been used to bail out uninsured depositors of that type before.
The record of the Government has been rather abysmal. Just the other day, I read with interest the October 1986 issue of a magazine entitled Policy Options. It would make good reading for Members of Parliament because it goes on to describe the impact of taxes in vivid detail. As a matter of fact, it almost makes one break down after finding out what is happening to the poor and middle-income families of Canada. It discusses the massive tax increases imposed on the average Canadian family. The middle-income group is being squeezed and squeezed at the same time as tax breaks are going to upper-income earners, those who are most likely to take advantage of the $500,000 capital gains exemption and the changes to the Registered Retirement Savings Plan. If a person happens to have $15,000 lying around at the end of the year, he can put it away tax free. How many of your constituents, Madam Speaker, have $15,000 at the end of the year to invest in retirement? If they do have $15,000 in cash to invest, ought we not use our tax system through a tax deferral program to assist that handful of individuals provide for their retirement?
The point I am trying to make is that at the same time as we are giving break after break to upper-income earners, we are hammering away at the middle-income earners. We are hammering away at the poor. The number of poor people is increasing while the middle class is decreasing. At the same time, when you shift your attention to the corporate side, you find the effective tax rate paid by small companies is higher than that of large companies. As a result of various tax breaks, thousands and thousands of profitable Canadian corporations do not pay tax. We have a long list of companies in the $50 million to $300 million profits range which have paid no income tax at all. That is why the Government slaps on to the backs of ordinary Canadians a whole range of new taxes such as we see in Bill C-14.
The rather sad aspect of all this is that these taxes are not out in front for everyone to see. In a sense we are not being honest. We are not being accountable. What we are levying as a result of this Bill's passage is a whole set of under-the-table, sneaky, behind-the-door taxes. The person paying the taxes is, by and large, unaware of it. If we believe in our tax system, if we want to be accountable for our deeds, it is imperative that we put in place a progressive, not a regressive, tax system. People should pay according to their ability to pay. If you have a large income, you can expect to pay a bit more tax. If you have a very low income, then in many cases you should be paying no income tax whatsoever. That is the kind of tax system a progressive country should have.
I will simply say in closing that we will continue to speak against this Bill. We will do what we can to encourage government Members to see their folly in the hope that the Government will see fit to withdraw the Bill.

Member wants to add to the number of social programs, how is he going to pay for them?
He knows that in Manitoba an NDP Government thinks nothing of taxing small business. They think nothing of doing that when they can take advantage of it. Where is the NDP's principles is the question I would like to ask the Hon. Member.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the intervention by my hon. friend. I will do my best to respond.
There were a number of questions. The point I want to make right off the mark is that when I refer to the fact that there are 79,196 Canadian corporations not paying tax, I do not
October 30, 1986

necessarily say those individual companies have done anything wrong at all.
Most of them are small.

A lot of them are relatively small businesses, yes. They are simply using the tax system which successive Liberal and Conservative Governments have put in place. They are not doing anything wrong by using what the duly-elected Government of Canada has given them to use. They will presumably take advantage of the $15,000 retirement program and are not doing anything wrong, just simply taking advantage of a silly program.
You would take it away from them?

What I am saying is that it is wrong in principle when we go out and gouge the taxpayer time and time again. We have done that so many times in the last two years since the Progressive Conservative Government took over-
Not true and you know it.

-more than any other time in Canadian history. Some $1,350 in increased taxes for the average family. He did not say that.
I hope he is not saying that.
What about Manitoba?

The Hon. Member made the point that, presumably, there are some difficult times in Manitoba. If my recollection is correct, when the unemployment figures came out last month, the Province of Manitoba had the lowest level of any province in the country. There were also some statistics from the Department of Finance recently which said that there was more business investment per capita in the Province of Manitoba than in any other province in Canada. The Hon. Member stands in his place and presumably implies they are having some difficult times. They are not perfect. What I am saying is that there is more corporate investment per capita in Manitoba than in any other place in Canada and unemployment is the lowest in any place in Canada. He should be leaping to his feet and congratulating that province's Government, saying it has done an excellent job and thank you very much.
Excise Tax Act

Madam Speaker, this Bill will certainly not implement tax reform, as the Hon. Member and others have pointed out. However, in recent weeks the Government has spoken about tax reform. Considering what has been done over the last two years to gouge middle and low-income taxpayers, to talk about tax reform now seems a bit incongruous.
Perhaps the Hon. Member mentioned this in his speech and I did not hear it, but does he believe it would be a good idea, considering the promise of the Government to bring in tax reform, to suspend these measures altogether until we see what the Government has in mind specifically, or, as an alternative, make this a temporary Bill as from time to time some tax measures have been made. It would be timed to expire in one year's time or two years' time. We can then seriously work on tax reform. To vote for a Bill like this while there is talk of tax reform appears to be contradictory.
I would also like to know whether the Hon. Member, as a principal representative of the NDP, takes the position that before we discuss tax reform there should be some direction from the Government. It should not simply be saying, as it did in answer to a question the other day, that it is not putting any kind of paper or direction before the Canadian people as to where it would like to go. It is consulting without any paper on the table and it is just going to listen. In any case, I would like to hear the views of the Hon. Member on those questions.

Madam Speaker, I know how hard the Hon. Member works in his constituency and that he is well aware of the problems of his constituents. The people of his constituency are almost unanimously overtaxed. Whether you are a small business owner, an employee in a large or small company, or self-employed, you are overtaxed. We have taxed people too much. Therefore, I agree with the Hon. Member that to proceed with this with the promise of tax reform around the corner is inappropriate.
I am going to attempt to predict the future. I know that is a shaky business. However, I believe that you will see the biggest con job that you have ever seen in your life. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has not called this the business transfer tax for no reason. He wants to give the impression that the business transfer tax is a tax on business. Rather than raise ' corporate rates or remove some of the most obvious corporate loopholes, he will simply say that the Government is levying a new business transfer tax which, as you well know, Madam Speaker, is not a business transfer tax but a fancy value-added or sales tax.
If the Government was committed to real and comprehensive tax reform, it would not be proceeding with Bill C-14 as it is before us today. This is one of the most regressive and backward- looking comprehensive sales taxes that has been introduced in a long time.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, thank you for this opportunity to take part in the debate today. In fact, I was somewhat reluctant because I thought the Conservative Government would have realized it had to change its approach and that today in the House, we would hear Conservative Members being more straightforward about the disastrous effects these budgetary measures would have on Canadians.
I was disappointed, though not surprised, when not a word was said today by Conservative Members about this budgetary measure, and I am referring to Bill C-14.

Yesterday in the House of Commons the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Vincent) presented this Bill to us. We were all here listening very attentively to him. Most of us were listening with great anticipation, hoping that the Parliamentary Secretary would present an unbiased, non-partisan view of this Bill, listing all its benefits. Instead, he spoke only very briefly about what the Bill would do. He said:
The purpose of this Bill is to increase federal sales tax in certain areas. An increase of 1 per cent will raise sales tax on construction materials from 7 to 8 per cent, on alcohol and tobacco from 14 to 15 per cent and on other commodities from 11 to 12 per cent.
He then went on to compliment the Tory Government and say all kinds of other partisan things. That is about all he said about the Bill. We are in the House again today waiting with great anticipation for another Conservative Member to explain to us in detail the positive benefits of this piece of legislation. However, that has not been forthcoming and that is very unfortunate. I would like to read some of the partisan remarks which the Parliamentary Secretary made yesterday. He said:
As you know, Mr. Speaker, last week the Auditor General presented his report in which he referred to the spendthrift habits of the previous administration and pointed out how they wasted Canadian taxpayers' money for unduly partisan ventures, but the people were not fooled and we turfed them right out.
Can you believe that a Tory made a remark like that, Madam Speaker? I am sure you are surprised that such a remark was made in this House, and I do not blame you. 1 am totally dumbfounded that a Conservative would have the unmitigated gall to make such remarks and I know you are as well. He went on to apologize for some of these taxes in his usual conservative way and said:
On one hand, we increase certain taxes in areas where it is reasonable to do so-
Please bear in mind the words "reasonable to do so". I will tell you the true story of what will really happen. I have a table in my hand which indicates the net effects of Bill C-14. A family of four with one breadwinner earning $15,000 a year will have their taxes increased by 1.7 per cent. Do you think a family of four with one breadwinner earning $15,000 a year can afford to pay any more money to the Tories? Surely not. I know that you understand that.
A family of four earning $50,000 a year will have increased taxes of 1.2 per cent. How can it be fair that someone earning $50,000 a year ends up paying a proportionately smaller increase than someone earning $15,000 a year who has the same size of family? I will now turn to another situation.

A single-parent family with two children and an income of $20,000 per year would see its taxes increased by 2.1 per cent. A single-parent family, $20,000 per year and two children.
Now consider the pitiful circumstances of a person with an income of $100,000 per year. A married couple, one breadwinner, two children, $100,000 per year. I realize the Conservatives think these people are much to be pitied. But consider. This family's taxes will increase by 1.7 per cent this year. This means that with an annual income of $100,000, you get a better deal from this Government than when you have an annual income of $20,000 as a single parent, a mother with two children. And why? Remember what the Parliamentary Secretary said.
October 30, 1986

Remember that the Parliamentary Secretary said that "we increase certain taxes in areas where it is reasonable to do so". It is the view of the Parliamentary Secretary that it is reasonable to do that which I have just described. Let me read more of what he said. Since he is a Parliamentary Secretary, presumably what he said in the House of Commons must be Conservative policy and that he believed it to be accurate. He said:
All families whose income is under $15,000 a year will be entitled to a tax credit... A family of four earning less than $15,000 will get a $150 tax credit.
The Parliamentary Secretary congratulates himself and the Conservative Government in an attempt to have Canadians believe that the family of four earning less than $15,000 a year will get some benefit from the Government. The net effect, however, is not that a family of four will be $150 richer, it will end up $255 poorer.

Well, let me explain, Madam Speaker, because I know I am stirring your curiosity. Here we are. Here is this family of four I was referring to, if we add the 3 per cent de-indexation of income tax, the 5 and 10 per cent surtax, the elimination of the 1973 deduction, changes to family allowances, the income tax credit and the exemption, all this adds up to a $190 tax increase. The 1 per cent sales tax increase in 1984, the 1 per cent sales tax increase in 1985, the widening of the sales tax base, higher alcohol and tobacco taxes amount to a $175 increase per year for that family of four earning $15,000 a year.
As far as the capital gains exemption is concerned, I may safely say that for people with a $15,000 a year income, earning capital gains means that they have to have some sort of capital. The odds are they do not have any, but let us assume they gain $10 on that. The February 1986 Budget that increased the surtax by 3 per cent, that increased this family's costs by $10, the income tax refund the Parliamentary Secretary was bragging about yesterday, all this amounts to a $150 reduction. That is true. And, finally, the 1 percent sales tax increase in the February 1986 Budget increased the whole package by 40 per cent.

Mr. Speaker, Madam Speaker, I followed with considerable interest the speech we heard a few moments ago. You have ruled on the relevance of certain material. The public at large and Hon. Members of the House are quite capable of reading the daily newspaper, page 18, and drawing their own conclusions.
The Hon. Member draws attention to the fact that there are people in the country who live below the poverty line and who are in difficulty. This is quite so, and no one disputes that fact. However, it is interesting to review some of the matters that have occurred which have assisted in adding to this number. For many years we have had increasing deficits. In fact, they amounted to tens of billions of dollars during the time that the party of the Hon. Member was in government. A series of reports by Auditors General clearly indicated that the financial management of the country was completely out of control. It was recommended again and again by these Auditors General that measures should be instituted to deal with this matter. Nothing was done until the last Auditor General's Report which was tabled in the House last week. It must be very difficult indeed. With respect to taxes and the increases in taxes which Bill C-14 represents, I would like to say something about how I regret that taxes, even regressive taxes such as sales taxes, are not used more selectively and for other purposes. I am referring here to a matter I raised in the House, I believe just last week, with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) concerning taxes on leaded and unleaded gasoline.
In this Bill, as in others, there are opportunities for the Government to use the tax system as an instrument of other goals, in this case an ecological goal, an environmental goal. Personally, I cannot understand why. I cannot see the logic of why the Government has refused to equalize the price of leaded and unleaded gasoline through the tax system.
A great hurrah has been made about the goal of the Government to get rid of leaded gasoline by 1992. At the same time, it should be acknowledged that the Royal Society recommended to the Government in its study that this be done by 1990. Nevertheless, the Government has set 1992 as its goal. I wish it were earlier, but it is not. In the meantime, the
October 30, 1986

very least that could be done, which is not a big deal, is simply to reduce the incentive that exists at the pumps for Canadians to use leaded gasoline. People are misfuelling now and using leaded gasoline when they should be using unleaded gasoline in order to save the difference between the price of leaded gasoline and unleaded gasoline. I cannot for the life of me understand why the government doesn't act on this.
The Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) said that the continued use of leaded gasoline-and he used the words- was like arsenic in your children's food. That is not something said by some grandstanding opposition Member. That was said by the Minister of the Environment. Surely if that is the case, and I do not think that it is too extravagant an analogy, the least we could do would be to have a tax system that discouraged people from doing that type of thing. I think it bears repeating, and 1 will repeat it at every opportunity, that I cannot understand why the tax system is not used in that way. If we must have regressive sales taxes and other hidden taxes, why can they not at least be used for some worthy social or environmental goal?
Another one that comes to mind is the tax on recycled oil. Many things are said about conservation and the need to recycle. Yet, if my memory serves correctly, at one point there was no tax on recycled oil. Now there is. I forget when that tax came into being. I cannot even say whether it was the responsibility of the former Liberal Government or the Conservative Government. This is a tax which should be lifted so that there is an incentive to make economic the reuse of certain substances, in this case used oil, so that we do not, as a result of those types of products being uneconomic, have them dumped down the sewers, or disposed of in other environmentally unacceptable ways.
I raise those two examples. I can think of other ways in which sales taxes and other taxes could be used to make cheaper those things which would be environmentally better for people to use, and to make more expensive those things which are damaging to the environment. That in the end is not the solution. I acknowledge that it simply means that those who can afford it can continue to do the environmentally damaging thing, and those who cannot will through the tax system be forced to be more responsible than they otherwise might.
I do not suggest it as a total solution, but I do suggest it as a way of doing things which a Progressive Conservative Government in particular might embrace. It is comparable to a market mechanism. It still leaves the choice with people, rather than doing what those awful socialists might do and making it impossible for people to do the wrong thing by legislating against it. I say to the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker), who is in the chair now, who is known for his rants against the socialists, that I am making a suggestion to him and to his colleagues that I think should find some favour with them. What it means is that Canadians, men and women alike, will have to pay $6 billion more between now and 1990. For this year alone, 1986, an additional load of $820 million: the 1 per cent increase in the sales tax will cost Canadian taxpayers $700 million, the increase in taxes on alcohol another $125 million, and two minor changes will translate into an additional $5 million reduction. According to the figures tabled by the Minister and according to conservative estimates, which reflect the Government's philosophy, for the excise tax alone, we have to add another $5 billion, or $1 billion a year multiplied by two, since there was a 2 per cent increase, which means $10 billion.

people would not realize what they are paying in taxes and the effect that this can have on their purchasing power. These are decisions made by the Conservative Government.

If we consider the statements made to the press on July 18 and the speech made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in Washington-I am of course referring to the Minister of Finance of Canada and what he said in Washington-and we draw a parallel with what appears on pages 52 and 53 of the Budget Papers of February 26, Madam Speaker, I would say that even someone with the best of intentions who would set out to make a purely objective analysis of the Government's policy, well that person would be in for a big surprise, because after trying to make a completely impartial judgment of the Minister's statements, this person would fail to understand why. ever since September 4, 1984, the Government's tax measures have been the exact opposite of what was said by the Minister on July 18 and in his speech in Washington.
I have just spoken about the sales tax and the philosophy it reflects. Now, I would like to say a few words about two other matters, personal income tax and measures affecting corporations.
If we look only at the effects of the 1986 Budget-I am setting aside for now the 1985 Budget, which resulted in an increase of billions of dollars because of the partial de-indexing of taxation tables and the 5 and 10 per cent surtax applied to Canadian taxpayers-if we look only at the effect of the Budget brought down on February 26, 1986, we find that the cumulative effect of this Budget on personal income tax will be a net increase of $100 million in 1986, $700 million in 1987, $800 million in 1988, something over $800 million in 1989 and $900 million in 1990. We therefore have an increase of $3.3 billion in personal income tax.
I trust that no one will be shocked to learn by how much corporate income taxes will increase during the same period. The increase will amount to $240 million in 1986, $270 million in 1987, $80 million in 1988, $175 million in 1989, and $50 million in 1990. Here again, Mr. Speaker, the impact on corporations is not due to any change which might have increased corporate income taxes. It is due only to the structural effect of the measures announced by the Conservative Government. In other words, the 3 per cent inventory allowance was suddently removed, which represents a substantial and immediate tax increase. However, since this is compensated by a decrease in tax rates, the net effect mentioned by the Minister of Finance, either directly or through his officials, would be nil. In other words, the impact of the February 26, 1986 Budget on individuals will be a $3 billion increase, whereas in the case of corporations, taking into account the consequences I have just mentioned, will be something less than $1 billion, and in the long term it will have no effect at all. In a nutshell, here is what the Minister of Finance has done since he took over on the advent of the Mulroney Government: direct and indirect taxes on individuals have increased considerably, $3 billion in personal income tax in the February 1986 Budget alone, not to mention the share these same taxpayers have to fork over in federal sales tax when they buy Canadian made goods. In the meantime corporate taxes went down, so when the Minister of Finance

October 30, 1986
Excise Tax Act
comes into the House to make a statement on tax reform and pretends that the purpose of the whole exercise is equity, neutrality, justice and what have you-the kind of words we find in any dictionary and hear from the pulpit, on Sundays usually-we can see that it is the other way around altogether.
So why now? Madam Speaker, you will understand why we on this side of the House, and I especially, have tried on several occasions to have the Minister of Finance come clean and tell us exactly just where he is leading us with his tax reform. I asked questions about the surtax or the $500,000 capital gains tax exemption. I tried to find out which exemptions he wanted to abolish to lighten the onus of tax legislation on Canadian taxpayers. We could not get answers! How can we enter upon a loyal, bona fide discussion with this Government when the only reference we can use is the impact of the May 1985 Budget and the February 1986 Budget that are completely-as far apart as the North Pole and the South Pole, with all that difference between the two.
Madam Speaker, if you add the additional effect on personal income tax, the impact of the May 1985 Budget, the cumulative effect by the end of 1990 would not be $3.3 billion, but many more billions of dollars. This is why you will understand easily that on this side of the House we will oppose Bill C-14. We will vote against it. We are going to use all available means to draw the Canadian taxpayer's attention to the most harmful effects of this legislation. Not only are they harmful as such, but they are totally at odds with the statements made by the Minister of Finance on July 18, in his Washington speech.
Madam Speaker, you may rest assured that not only here but also in committee my colleagues will question the Government and find out the actual impact of each clause of this Bill which is of such consequence for the Canadian taxpayers.

Madam Speaker, I indicated earlier that I was willing to approach a tax reform as fairly and objectively as I could. But I ask the Hon. Member who put the question: What should I take a stand on since nothing has been brought forward?
All we had from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is what I would call a motherhood and apple pie statement. There was no concrete proposal.
I could return the question to the Hon. Member for Chicoutimi and ask what response could we give to the Business Council on National Issues, which recommends to the government to abolish the $500,000 exemption on capital gains tax.
Our stand has been from the beginning that this exemption is unfair.
Madam Speaker, what the Conservative have been saying about the deficit would make me laugh if it were not such a serious matter, because when I campaigned with my colleagues in 1984, we said we could not make foolish electoral promises considering the financial situation Canada was in as a result of the worldwide economic recession we experienced in 1981 and 1982. The hardship was felt not only in Canada but everywhere in the United States and in European countries, and the whole western world went through an economic crisis.
Perhaps I may answer his question with a question: Is the Conservative Party suggesting that in order to keep the deficit down during the recession in 1981-82, when thousands and thousands of workers were being affected, it would have been better for the Government to ignore these people, to make budget cuts and cut unemployment insurance and leave those unfortunates who lost their jobs as a result of the recession to their own devices? Is that their way of developing the economy and at the same time making their policies reflect a measure of social justice?
Personally, I think the decisions made in 1981-82 that had an impact on the deficit were decisions that had to be made. With hindsight, perhaps we would have done certain things differently. But the fact remains that there was every justification for government intervention.
And I would like to put the same question to the Hon. Member for Chicoutimi. Considering the economic recovery that started in 1983, halfway through 1983 and accelerated in 1984, when we had a GNP growth of 4.5 or 5 per cent, I want to ask him why, after almost three years of economic recovery, this Conservative Government which was going to solve all our problems has, in three years, managed to add $100 billion to the national debt?
October 30, 1986

You say it was $200 billion. For the last full year under the Liberal Government, our total national debt was $160 billion, and in three years you will have added $100 billion to that amount. Which means, dividing $100 billion by $260 billion, an increase of 50 per cent. However, I think all this is beside the point, not only as far as Bill C-14 is concerned but also if we consider the realities of our economy.
Look at the United States. There we have a President who was elected in 1980, when he promised to fight the deficit. This year, the United States will have the biggest deficit the U.S. economy has ever had, namely $220 billion.
That is why I wouldn't mind getting into some of the more detailed aspects, such as free trade and the party's position, and whenever the Minister and the Hon. Member for Chicoutimi care to have a debate on the subject, I am ready and willing. For the time being, however, we are talking about Bill C-14, and its effects not just on the Canadian economy but on the taxpayer, and I am ready for any other questions within that context.

If we consider the cumulative effects, Madam Speaker, the figures are so high that an observer who has not read the small print in the legislation that have been passed and who is not familiar with the two Budgets might think that the Member of the Official Opposition is juggling with figures

which do not make sense and are beyond reality. On the contrary, and I want to assure all those who are listening here in the House or watching television that the figures are for real. The cost in 1986-87, the cumulative effect of the two Budgets represents a little over $5 billion for Canadian taxpayers. This includes the 3 per cent de-indexation in the tax tables, the 3 per cent surplus, $570 million. There was a 5 and 10 per cent surtax which Conservative Members may have chosen to ignore and, if we combine this with the elimination of the 1973 tax exemption, we are looking at another $1 billion. When the Business Council and National Issue deals with this matter, I have to admit to the Hon. Member for Ottawa- Vanier that indeed it is quite a realistic approach. If we were to sum up this document we realize that the-and this is supposed to represent big business. The mouthpiece of the capitalists. I am beginning to wonder whether, from an ideological standpoint, the Conservative Members and the Conservative Government might not stand to the right of the major Canadian corporations.
Do you know what major Canadian corporations are recommending? That the $500,000 capital gains tax exemption be abolished, and the ones who are making this recommendation are those who could benefit from this exemption since they can make investments which will bring them capital gains. It is not someone with an income of $15,000 or $20,000 who can afford to invest in the stock market and have capital gains.
Another interesting aspect of this is that the Conservative Government has announced changes to pension plans as concerns what can be invested in registered retirement savings plans. This system is also helpful. I have nothing against investing in RRSP's. But what people tell us is that such measures benefit the wealthy more than the poor and that a policy which has just been announced should now be changed to make it more equitable. This should be replaced by tax credits.
Madam Speaker, the question asked by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier was very relevant and it gave me an opportunity to add a few comments to what I said some minutes ago.

These proposals are the latest in a series of tax measures brought in by the Government and the Minister which have

October 30, 1986
Excise Tax Act
increased the sales and excise taxes and have cost every family in this country $1,300 since the Government took office.
Let me tell the Hon. Member for Seikirk-Interlake (Mr. Holtmann), who intervened in this debate to defend the $500,000 exemption on capital gains, that for every one of his constituents who will benefit from that measure, he has 100 or 200 constituents who cannot afford to pay that $1,305 increase in family taxes which the Government has imposed.

Those facts are correct. Spain, Portugal and Italy are doing much better than before. We should keep the record straight.
We should keep the record straight with respect to taxation. After listening to the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills I think he would call anyone to the left of Genghis Kahn a socialist. He should be current and understand what has happened in the last month in the United States, which has its most conservative president in 50 years. They have turned their tax system around and have cut the rate of corporation taxes and the rate for personal income taxes, without increasing excise taxes but by closing the loopholes on corporate taxes and personal income taxes.
The Hon. Member talked about capital gains tax. We have made it very clear that we do not oppose farmers and small business people being able to turn their farms and their businesses over to their children without having to pay capital gains tax. I point out to the Hon. Member that in its most recent tax change bills, the United States has increased rather than decreased the rate at which people pay taxes on any capital gains they make. The Hon. Member should at least be current and look for advice from the very people whom he has lauded so often.
We are opposed to this Bill because it continues the process which the Government began when it took office. In November of 1984, the Minister of Finance in his economic statement announced an increase of 1 per cent in federal sales tax. That is something the Liberals had proposed and the Conservatives had opposed when they were in opposition. The petroleum compensation charge was increased.
In his May 1985 Budget, the Minister of Finance increased the federal sales tax by another 1 per cent effective January 1, 1986. He increased the excise tax on gasoline. He implemented a new excise tax of 2 cents per litre on diesel and aviation fuel. He broadened the federal sales tax base to include candy, confectionary, soft drinks and pet food. I wonder what he has against the kids who like candy? He increased the excise tax on tobacco and on alcohol.
In his Budget of February 1986, the Minister of Finance increased the federal sales tax as of April 1, 1986 by another 1 per cent. He increased the excise tax on tobacco and on alcohol. We have calculated that those tax increases cost every family $1,305.
At the same time, the Minister of Finance was permitting, as has the United States for many years, some of the largest corporations in the United States and Canada to get away without paying any sales tax at all. The Citizens for Tax Justice in the United States has compiled its annual list of corporate taxpayers or what they call "corporate free-loaders". It is no surprise to me that not only are many of the top 10 corporate free-loaders not paying any taxes but are receiving tax rebates. They are getting money back.
The top 10 companies in the United States had a profit of $39.6 billion from 1982 to 1985 and received a rebate of $1.5 billion for an effective tax rate of minus 3.8 per cent. I would like to put on the record some of those companies. Boeing Company between 1980 and 1985 made profits of $2.25 billion. It received a tax rebate of $121 million. Pepsi Cola received a rebate of $89.3 million. DuPont received a tax rebate of $179 million. Texaco received a tax rebate of $68 million. International Paper received a tax rebate of $59.8 million.
The Government is congratulating itself because it sold-I believe it gave-de Havilland to Boeing. Boeing in the United States, as I indicated, paid no corporate tax at all. I am worried that Boeing in Canada will be permitted by the Minister of Finance and the Government to do in Canada what it did in the United States, that is pay no taxes at all.
We must ask the Minister of Finance if that is the kind of fair tax system he talks about. The illustrations I have given about what has happened in the United States can be duplicated over and over again in Canada. Our research tells us that there are a whole host of companies, some of them the largest corporations in Canada, which in the five years from 1980 to
October 30, 1986

1985 paid no taxes at all in at least one of those years. Let me detail some of these corporations.
The Royal Bank and the Bank of Montreal paid no taxes at all. There is not an employee of either of those banks who has not paid income tax, but the companies they work for have made hundreds of millions of dollars in profits and paid no taxes at all. The Hudson's Bay Company, the Thompson financial interest, is among the largest and wealthiest groups in the world. It owns oil companies, newspapers, television stations, and retail stores, yet paid no taxes at all. The Power Corporation and some of its groups, and the Investors' Group, paid no taxes at all in at least one of five years I mentioned. I could go on and on, Madam Speaker. I am sure Conservative Members of Parliament know a good deal more about the Roman Corporation and Mr. Roman than I do. He has become one of the wealthiest people in Canada. I do not object to his doing well if he is aggressive and clever and adds something, as he does, to the productive capacity of this country. However, I think that as long as ordinary citizens, some of them making very little over the minimum wage, have to pay income taxes and the kinds of sales and excise taxes I have talked about, it is only fair to say to Mr. Roman, and to the hundreds like Mr. Roman, that they should be paying their fair share of the taxes as well. We have not seen any desire on the part of the Minister of Finance or his Government to do that. What we have seen again and again is increases in taxes, many of them hidden. We are now talking about a business transfer tax, which is another form of sales tax but even more regressive than the previous sales taxes.
We have seen increases in taxes, usually hidden, as often as the Minister of Finance can figure out how to do it, which adds to the burden of the ordinary citizen, which cuts down on the real incomes and living standards of ordinary Canadians while at the same time encouraging and permitting those at the top to live ever better and better.
It is our intention, which will come as no surprise to Conservative Members of Parliament, to oppose this tax measure which we believe to be regressive and unfair, and we will continue to urge the people of Canada to demand a tax system which will be fair and one which will get the revenue the Government needs to provide the services from those who are best able to pay. The proposal contained in this Bill does the exact opposite. As we have done in the past and will do in the future, we intend to oppose and vote against passage of this Bill.
