subtopic: SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY-REQUEST FOR RESTORATION OF FUNDING. (B) BASIC RESEARCH FUNDING. (C) SCIENTISTS EMPLOYED BY COUNCIL
SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY-REQUEST FOR RESTORATION OF FUNDING. (B) BASIC RESEARCH FUNDING. (C) SCIENTISTS EMPLOYED BY COUNCIL
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on October 16 I asked the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) if the $20 million being cut from the National Research Council could be restored. Many of the programs of the National Research Council have been cut because of the desire of the Government to reduce the deficit. It seemed to me to be a modest request given the significance of the work carried on by the NRC and the manner in which the Government spends its money in other areas.
One can ask which is more important, spending $41 million more to move a prison to Port-Cartier or spending $20 million to keep NRC at a minimum strength to continue its programs. This question has been asked of me a number of times in a number of different ways. Why, for example, could not $20 million be found in the $1 billion for research for the universities which the Government keeps talking about?
This is a valid question, and one which the Government should seriously answer. As more persons become aware of what is happening at the NRC, they will see that panic cuts are shutting down entire programs in which huge amounts of capital have been invested in the past. This is no way to wind down research. It severely undercuts the resources available to the nation in terms of scientific expertise.
We know already that we will be losing a world-class observatory at Algonquin Park, and that the electromagnetic engineering section of NRC is being closed down despite its clear record of achievement in health areas that the Minister of State for Science and Technology said he would protect. We will know more about the effects of these cuts in the days ahead. In fact, each day brings a new horror story of how Canada is losing out again in an area in which the Government has promised major improvements in national performance in scientific research and development. After all, the Government promised that it would move to devoting 2.5 per cent of Gross National Product to scientific research and development.
The question I asked also raised the question of Dr. John Polanyi, our new Nobel Laureate in Chemistry, who began his distinguished career in Canada in post-doctoral work at the NRC. The Minister's response to my inquiry about giving future Canadian researchers the same opportunity that Dr. Polanyi had was to beg the question by saying that Dr. Polanyi had not worked for the NRC for some time and that he is now a professor at the University of Toronto.
The facts are these. Dr. Polanyi began his career in Canada. He came from Great Britain to the NRC. His lab is now being shut down as a direct result of these cuts. Dr. Polanyi greatly enjoyed his time at the NRC. In his own words: "It was a great place to do science". Dr. Polanyi now has great doubts about Canada's will or ability to support research. He said that if he were starting today: "I think I would go to the United

October 30, 1986
Adjournment Debate
States." Nothing could be more clear-cut about our decline in the eyes of those who know research work best.
It does no good for the Minister to say that Dr. Polanyi has endorsed the policies of this Government because he has not yet moved to the United States. Other universities have felt the brain-drain acutely, and it will be accelerating. When one examines it, the Government's five-year, $1 billion plan for university research means that matching grants from industry must fund additional research, otherwise funds for research are frozen and will decline.
No doubt Dr. Polanyi will have no trouble obtaining research funding now. But what about the future Polanyi's? What private sector corporation will have the wisdom and the funds to back them when they are unknowns trying to get started, as so many of them are?
For these and many other reasons I must go back to my first question. Will the Government find a fairly small amount- $20 million-so that valuable research and development in the national interest at the National Research Council can continue? Without it we may be at a research point of no return.
It is a final irony that the one university which seems to be suffering the most from lack of research funding is the University of Waterloo, a university which entered new fields of computer technology. Yet it is the whole nation which is watching and which will suffer from the Waterloo which the Government has reached in scientific research.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gordon Towers (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY-REQUEST FOR RESTORATION OF FUNDING. (B) BASIC RESEARCH FUNDING. (C) SCIENTISTS EMPLOYED BY COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to the Hon. Member, Dr. Polanyi worked at the National Research Council for two years ending in 1954. He then moved to the University of Toronto where most of his research was performed with extensive assistance from the Natural Science and Engineering Research Council. The success of his work there demonstrates the strength of supporting pure research at the universities.
The decision to scale down the NRC laboratory dealing with photochemistry and kinetics was made by the NRC's Executive Council after careful consideration of all programs. The photochemistry program at NRC has been wound down over the last decade as the science and technology has been transferred to industry and universities. Dr. Polanyi is himself an example of this development.
It should be remembered that Dr. Polanyi's connection with the laboratory is now 32 years old. He joined the laboratory in 1952 after completing his PhD. at the university of Manchester in England and worked there for two years before moving to the University of Toronto. While there he received increasing support from government granting programs. In fact, this year with $220,000 he is the largest single recipient of a research operating grant in the whole country.
The important thing we can learn from this is that world class basic research was done at a university with government support. This demonstrates the vitality of the government approach of supporting pure research at the universities. Basic research at the universities can be effective.
The Government wants to foster basic research at the universities because the graduate students involved in this effort come away with the most up-to-date experience possible. In many ways, it may be easier to perform such research in government laboratories, but then it has proven difficult to train people to use the results. Our new thrust is to move the performance to universities where training is an integral part of their job and the knowledge of outstanding researchers like Dr. Polanyi can be passed on.
This is a healthy shift in emphasis. We are not discontinuing all basic research at NRC and other government laboratories. It has its place there. But we are pushing more of it toward the universities. In 1950 only 19 universities received research assistance from the federal Government. That number has now increased to 52. The university sector represents a rich and varied pool of talent that is well able to undertake the increased work being sent its way. That is why earlier this year the Government took steps to preserve the funding level of the granting councils for the next five years, even in the face of the need to control spending wherever possible.
I must say that the alarmist attitude of the Hon. Member opposite does nothing for the research community in Canada.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-ASSISTANCE FOR GRAIN FARMERS. (B) ALLOCATION OF ASSISTANCE
AGRICULTURE-ASSISTANCE FOR GRAIN FARMERS. (B) ALLOCATION OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 8, 1986,1 directed a question to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and asked him about the $1 billion assistance program to grain farmers which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) mentioned a few days before. This was an interesting announcement by the Prime Minister. In the Speech from the Throne on October 1 there was no mention of the $1 billion of assistance.
Three or four days later when the Minister and the Prime Minister spoke in the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, the Prime Minister casually mentioned that the Government was going to provide assistance to farmers, that the amount of the assistance had been estimated at $1 billion, and that he was going to negotiate it with Premier Devine of Saskatchewan.
It was very interesting that that announcement came during the Prime Minister's speech. We assumed that it resulted from a sheer terror telephone conversation supposedly to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) from Premier Devine in the midst of the election campaign, and to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight). This precipitated the casual mention of $1 billion of assistance need. The Prime Minister followed this up on about October 8 saying that this was desperately needed by western farmers.
October 30, 1986

At the same time the Premier of Saskatchewan suggested that the assistance would be in the form of a cash deficiency payment. However, the Minister of Agriculture was saying that the assistance might be in the form of a loan or some other assistance. As a matter of fact, I am not sure whether the Minister of Agriculture ever said that it would be a cash deficiency payment. Time has passed, the election has gone by, and the whole matter seems to be going into limbo.
There have been meetings of Deputy Ministers. In fact a Deputy Minister returned from a meeting in Saskatchewan and announced that the benefits would be made available on the basis of 1986 crop production, which would mean that in Saskatchewan there would be a cash deficiency payment of $457 million. Of course the office of the federal Minister of Agriculture denied it. Everyone has looked with great interest at this $1 billion of assistance. In fact, some farmers have actually called it "Brian's bogus billion". No one seems able to find out whether the money exists, whether it will be paid as a deficiency payment, whether it will be a loan, or whether it will be a loan guarantee. In any event, time goes on and the Government continues to talk about meetings and discussions.
I had an opportunity to discuss the issue with a provincial Minister. Although these supposed consultations are taking place, he certainly did not know how the assistance would be paid. In one comment to the media the Minister of Agriculture said that the $35 million self-sufficiency program in Atlantic Canada, which he announced some time last summer, might be raised to $50 million. That was the only reference to how the money would be paid, whether it exists, whether it is new money, old money or whatever. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will be able to announce tonight that it is not "Brian's bogus billion" but in fact is a $1 billion cash deficiency payment.
In another exchange which I had with the Minister of Agriculture concerning the $1 billion assistance for Canadian grain farmers, I asked him whether it would be paid as a deficiency payment in order to reduce the obligation of the Government under the western grain stabilization fund. Knowledgeable observers of the grain trade have said that the Government would be obligated under that fund to pay about $1 billion for the 1986-87 crop year. In his report the Auditor General pointed out that the deficit in the western grain stabilization fund this year would be approximately $100 million. We were trying to clarify whether it was new money to decrease the obligation of the federal Government under the western grain stabilization fund.
The Minister said that it was not to reduce the Government's obligation under the fund. It seems that the $1 billion under this aid program will be brought in under an appropriation Bill or in some other way and will not be used to reduce the Government's obligation under the western grain stabilization fund.
Adjournment Debate
Provided that it is not a bogus offer on the part of the Government, grain farmers will be getting $1 billion of assistance as a result of the tremendous problem in national grain trading and pricing this year, perhaps the worst since the 1930s. As well, people in the western grain area or the Wheat Board area will be receiving $1 billion or whatever the western grain stabilization fund will pay out.
I know the Parliamentary Secretary, being a very illustrious Member of Parliament and having great responsibility in the field of agriculture, will want to announce in clear and decisive tones tonight exactly how much money will be paid, on what terms it will be paid, whether it will be a cash deficiency payment based upon deliveries of grain, whether it will be an acreage payment, and how it will be paid out in other parts of Canada. We look forward to his comments this evening.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-ASSISTANCE FOR GRAIN FARMERS. (B) ALLOCATION OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on October 3 of this year, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised a $1 billion assistance program for grain farmers who are being affected by the subsidy war between the EEC and the United States. The measure had hardly been announced when the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) asked us to put the cart before the horse and announce how much farmers in his riding would receive and when.
I am sorry to disappoint him, but we want to act responsibly and consult with the main parties concerned before going any further. To this end, the Prime Minister announced in the House that the federal Government will be consulting with the farmers and the provinces before taking any action. We want to improve self-financing for farmers in the most effective and equitable way possible. I think that is pretty clear.
The so-called subsidy war between the EEC and the United States has created a national problem which requires the right national solution. Instead of going out and spend, spend and spend as the Hon. Member for Algoma would have us do, we want to consult with farmers' organizations and act in consultation with the provinces.
For some time we have been discussing with the provinces how best to help our grain farmers. In Victoria, on August 27 of this year, the Agriculture Ministers of all governments made a commitment to intervene in this area, in order to assist the agricultural sector and protect industry-related jobs throughout the country.
Following this meeting, the Ministers asked their officials to formulate recommendations on ways to assist the farmers affected by this subsidy war.
Madam Speaker, these recommendations were discussed at a meeting on October 9 in Ottawa. The provincial deputy ministers of Agriculture then pursued this task by assessing all options for countering the harmful effects of these subsidies.

October 30, 1986
Adjournment Debate
Perhaps the Hon. Member for Algoma would care to hear what the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) told them at the beginning of this meeting, and I quote:
We are not excluding any options. We are asking you to help us identify the best and most equitable ways of giving farmers the assistance they need.
Madam Speaker, the meeting was held less than a week after the Prime Minister's announcement. We believe quick action is necessary but also that we should think and consult before we spend. The Prime Minister has announced that the federal Government will increase the farmers' cash flow by about $1 billion. This new federal aid comes in addition to assistance already available under existing programs and will not involve reallocation of funds earmarked for other farm programs.
I said earlier that we are facing a problem which affects all farmers throughout this country. A national problem calls for a national response, and this is why I believe our initiative will take into account a wide range of farm products and various needs. The situation is clear and we have shown that we are prepared to take action. No option has been left aside. We are now looking at all possible solutions in co-operation with the main interest groups. Given the circumstances, this process is quite reasonable.
This week the Minister of Agriculture will have consultations with the leaders of our major farm organizations. I expect you will be there. Later on this month he will be meeting with his provincial counterparts, for the same reason.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT-PRIVATE SECTOR JOB CREATION-MINISTER'S STATEMENT. (B) TRAINING OF WORKERS

speechtext:
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Madam Speaker, on October 7, I asked the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) if his speech of October 6 in reply to the Speech from the Throne was a forecast of a further withdrawal from employment creation by the Conservative Government and of further cut-backs in job creation programs. The Minister did not answer my question and consequently I scheduled this debate for this evening.
[DOT]	0820)
In his speech of October 6 the Minister strongly suggested that the private sector, the provinces and individuals should have the principal responsibility for job training and job creation. That was nothing new. What was new was for the first time, at least that I recall, a Minister was saying it. Up until that time Ministers were saying that they were committed to job creation and job training but doing the opposite.
The Minister and his predecessor had already taken steps to abdicate their role in job creation. In the spending Estimates there was a reduction of $300 million from 1984 to 1986 in job creation funds, approximately 27 per cent when inflation is taken into account. The number of employment centres has
been cut, including specialty employment centres at universities. The number of people counselled by the Department has been cut. When an unemployed person seeks counselling with respect to employment, only about 20 per cent are given interviews and registered. The others are referred to bulletin boards where they are directed to look for work. There have been cuts in unemployment insurance, post-secondary education, and institutional training in the Department.
All this is happening at a time when 1.2 million people are unemployed. The Government maintains there have been improvements and of course the rate of unemployment has declined since the pit of the recession in 1983. However, it is still 9.5 per cent nationally. In Atlantic Canada it is nearly 15 per cent; in Quebec, 10.7 per cent; in the rich Province of Alberta, 9.9 per cent, higher than the national average; in British Columbia, 12.3 per cent. Youth unemployment is still approximately 15 per cent. While the Government claims it is doing well, there is still much to be done and this is no time to cut back on job-creation programs and leave it to other people.
In 1981, the year before the recession, unemployment was 7.5 per cent, and that should be the goal. In the period between 1965 and 1980, the average rate of unemployment was 5.6 per cent. That is a goal which should be pursued by the Government before it starts cutting employment programs. Part-time employment as a percentage of total employment has increased from 9 per cent in 1980 to 18 per cent in 1986. Those unemployed for more than a year is double in 1986 what it was in 1983, and four times the rate in 1981.
My conclusion is that if you look at all these statistics which I have referred to, this is no time to be cutting back on these programs. It is no time to be sloughing off the federal Government's responsibility. It is no time to tell individuals, the private sector and the provinces that this is their primary responsibility and the federal Government has nothing to do with it; or, if the Government does not go that far, that its role is not the principal role. It is, and the Government should return to the budgets and commitments it had when it came into office in 1984. This is no time to withdraw.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for External Relations):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT-PRIVATE SECTOR JOB CREATION-MINISTER'S STATEMENT. (B) TRAINING OF WORKERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when the Minister says that "practical training and job experience lead to permanent jobs", I fail to see what is wrong with his statement because this is what the new reality of job creation is all about.
My colleague opposite says that our job creation programs are necessarily geared to training, he claims that this is not a new approach, but he is quite wrong. It was a new approach indeed, the new job creation programs had to be geared to training, and this is how we got results. Members opposite do admit there have been results, but my colleague seems to imply that they were nothing but a by-product of improvement in the world economic situation. This is unfair, it was due to concerted action on the part of all interest groups, private and public
October 30, 1986

promoters alike, they all co-operated and managed to overcome the greatest danger we faced when we took office, a danger which is becoming smaller with time.
I agree with my colleague, we should strive for even lower unemployment rates. We all agree on that, but one thing is clear: whatever one may say or do, it is a fact that since September 1984 our job creation programs and policies have been successful, unemployment did go down. There are fewer unemployed. The unemployment rate has declined. And when people say that we pay less for unemployment insurance, it is obvious. I, for one, would like to pay nothing for unemployment insurance. That would mean full employment. Therefore, if people say that the Government is paying less, I am obviously happy. If we are paying less, it is because more people are
Adjournment Debate
working, which is what Canadian men and women want to achieve. This is why we have instituted new programs featuring compulsory training. Challenge '85 was a success, Challenge '86 was an even greater success since even student summer jobs were career oriented, and you can be sure that Challenge '87 will be better still!
